Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney will ride for Lidl-Trek from 2027.

The 32-year-old superstar and her incoming team confirmed a two-year deal Tuesday in a bombshell announcement that will tilt the landscape of the women’s peloton.

Niewiadoma-Phinney, a former winner of the Tour de France Femmes, has consistently proven she’s the best of the rest behind Demi Vollering .

The Polish attacker finished second behind Vollering this year at both the Tour de France Femmes and the recent road world championships. Their rich, long-running rivalry is one of the defining narratives of the modern sport.

After spending close to a decade at Canyon-SRAM, Niewiadoma-Phinney will bring Lidl-Trek a new talisman for the next two years.

Her GC and classics prowess will complement the squad’s current leaders Niamh Fisher-Black, Elisa Balsamo, and the prodigious Holmgren twins.

Beyond that, her arrival will boost the ambitious, cash-rich Lidl-Trek team into a bubbling “super team” battle that’s brewing at the top of the Women’s WorldTour. Vollering’s FDJ-Suez team and its challengers SD Worx-Protime and UAE ADQ have split into a separate echelon in recent years.

With Spanish super-talent Paula Blasi reportedly also leaving UAE for Movistar, the women’s peloton will race to a different beat next year.

Niewiadoma-Phinney acknowledged Tuesday she’s making a bold mid-career move in stepping away from Canyon-SRAM after nine years on its books.

“I am super excited about the next two years,” she said Tuesday.

“I have spent many years on the same team. The decision to move forward and change the environment wasn’t easy until I talked to Lidl-Trek. Instantly, I felt the team had a plan, trust and belief in me. I knew that when we joined forces we could aim for the highest dreams.

“I’m looking forward to working with people and professionals who have a fresh look at my abilities and at what we can achieve together, being guided from a different perspective and just new fresh air,” Niewiadoma-Phinney continued.

“I’m looking forward to learning from the team, what we can improve, how we can get faster and how we can raise our hands more often when crossing the finish line.”

No details were provided regarding Niewiadoma’s deal, but her palmarès will presumably push her pay toward the top end of the women’s peloton.

Vollering is thought to boast a seven-figure salary from FDJ-Suez that currently makes her the best-paid rider in the women’s peloton.

Lidl-Trek women’s team has also confirmed the signing of Arlenis Sierra, Ally Wollaston, and Julia Kopecký for 2027.

It’s a significant roster refresh, but one that’s dwarfed by what’s going on at the partnering men’s team.

Lidl-Trek men’s team has been on a huge WorldTour spending spree in recent months. Felix Gall, Jordan Jegat, and Jordi Meeus are the headliners of the seven names they’ve confirmed for the new season so far.

Davide Piganzoli (Visma-Lease a Bike) leads world champ Brandon McNulty (UAE Team Emirates - XRG) during the Giro dell'Emilia 2026 (Photo: Dario Belingheri/Getty Images) (Photo: @DarioBelingheri/@GettyImages)

Davide Piganzoli ran out the surprise winner of the Giro dell’Emilia on Saturday, benefiting from the same dedicated teamwork from Matteo Jorgenson that Brandon McNulty enjoyed at last weekend’s world championships.

Just as he did for McNulty, Jorgenson proved the kingmaker for Visma-Lease a Bike teammate Piganzoli after he launched a perfectly-timed solo attack in the finale.

The Italian made his move on a downhill with 4.8km to go, quickly gaining time while Jorgenson sat on wheels and marked all attempts to chase.

He started the final ascent of the San Luca climb with a 41 second lead and gave it everything on the 2.1km ascent, with Tom Pidcock (Pinarello Q36.5 Pro Cycling), Oscar Onley (Netcompany Ineos) and Ben Healy (EF Education EasyPost) all being marked by Jorgenson.

Pidcock leaped clear closer to the line and narrowed the gap to just two seconds, with Onley taking third. Jorgenson was fifth, 12 seconds back, while McNulty had a solid showing in his first outing in the rainbow jersey with tenth.

“I picked the right moment to attack, and it paid off,” Piganzoli said afterward. “We had several cards to play. We handled this race perfectly as a team. It means a lot to me to add this great race to my palmares.”

Although he won the recent Tour de Luxembourg, he looked far from the strongest on the penultimate ascent of the climb.

Jorgenson made his move there with 10.5km remaining, close to the summit, and went solo. Ben Healy (EF Education-EasyPost) brought back him before the top, with Onley also there, and on the descent they were joined by Pidcock and Piganzoli.

The latter made his move with 4.8km remaining, choosing the perfect moment. With Jorgenson blocking, he gained enough time to hold on until the end.

“I felt good in the closing kilometers, so I decided to go all in,” Piganzoli said. “I also wanted to put my teammates in a good position that way. We still had Ben behind us, who has a strong sprint.

“In the end, I was able to finish it off myself, but this was a victory for the entire team. I’m happy that I was able to show my good form from Luxembourg and the world championships here again.”

Saturday was the first chance for McNulty to show off his rainbow jersey and rainbow-adorned bike since his surprise win in last weekend’s world championships.

The steep gradients of the San Luca climb didn’t play to his strengths but he rode aggressively, going briefly clear with 19km to go and later remaining close to the lighter riders when they went all in with one lap to go. He ended up in the second chasing group on the road.

McNulty has made clear winning the worlds won’t prevent him from riding for team leader Tadej Pogačar and others, but he certainly performed strongly on Saturday. He eventually finished tenth, 45 seconds behind Piganzoli.

“Today was really special, racing in the rainbow jersey for the first time, and I enjoyed every moment of it,” he said afterwards.

“I gave everything last weekend at the world championships, so I knew I might still be missing a little bit today.

“It was a tough day out there, but there are still plenty of opportunities to come and I’m looking forward to the next races.”

McNulty is scheduled to ride the Coppa Agostoni on Sunday and then Tre Valli Varesine on Tuesday.

He is also expected to line out in Il Lombardia next Saturday, as is an in-form Jorgenson.

Tadej Pogačar is so desperate to race his “home” European championships in Ljubljana on Sunday that he’s putting pressure on his team to allow it.

At least, that’s according to reports from El País .

The Spanish paper reported Monday that Pogačar called the medic who operated on his busted collarbone four weeks ago in Barcelona. The Spanish paper wrote that the GOAT asked the surgeon Saturday for medical clearance to race the Euros this coming weekend, and was given the green light.

Pogačar is reportedly using that as backing for a conflict with his entourage at UAE Emirates-XRG, who are urging patience.

Pogačar broke his collarbone, a vertebra, and suffered a concussion when he crashed at 60kph last month at the Vuelta a España. It was a brutal fall that supposedly ended his season.

As Pogačar said at the time in a team statement, “This isn’t the way I wanted my season to finish. But right now, the most important thing is to recover properly and give my body the time it needs.”

If team brass buckles to Pogačar’s supposed wish to return, the 28-year-old will make a risky early comeback from his savage crash this very Sunday.

UAE Emirates-XRG told Velo on Tuesday morning that the reports out of Spanish media are “not true.”

Per El País , Pogačar has pulled a 180 from his previous acceptance that his season was over.

After missing the chance to defend his world title and being forced to watch his domestique Brandon McNulty win the rainbow bands, Pogačar is hungry to return to reimpose his rule over the peloton.

That’s contrary to his team’s ongoing reluctance to let him take any undue risk after such a hard crash.

But Pogačar has plenty of motivation to return to racing ASAP.

The European championships this weekend take place on his home soil. The course passes near his home town. He’s a national hero with home crowds to please. And he’s the defending European champion. His massive victory at last year’s race in the Ardéche is easily forgotten.

Pogačar’s home championship would be defizzed without him and his partner Urška Žigart , who’s also sidelined after she broke her jaw earlier this month.

Beyond that, the championship race against Remco Evenepoel (Paul Seixas confirmed he’s not starting) would serve as a test for Pogačar.

El País wrote he’s hungry to race Il Lombardia on October 10 to chase a record-breaking sixth victory in the falling leaves.

El País ’ reporting fuels a rumor that just keeps giving.

A mini storm of speculation blew up last week when Pogačar appeared on a provisional start list for Slovenia’s European champs.

At the time, UAE Emirates-XRG brushed it off.

“It’s probably an old list,” the team told Feltet . “Although he is back doing light indoor training, there are no plans for him to ride any more races this year.”

Since then, Pogačar has been bounding around looking chipper and race-ready.

He posted on Instagram on Saturday, sharing images from his first outdoor ride since La Vuelta , and his last day as world champion.

He looked fit and mobile as ever, and he’d not lost his sense of humor either.

The post includes a video of Pogačar comparing his fresh, palm-sized scar from collarbone surgery with his ride buddies, Eddie Dunbar and Zigart’s teammate, Gladys Verhulst-Wild.

UAE Emirates-XRG shut down the report from El País when Velo reached out for comment on Tuesday morning. “The article is not true,” wrote the team’s head of media.

Pogačar would be rolling the dice if he makes a comeback on Sunday.

He’s not a rider who shows up to roll around at the back of the bunch – he’ll be in his usual full superhero mode spraying attacks and railing descents.

El País reported that the surgeon told Pogačar on Saturday there’s no obstacle to him competing. But those healing fractures are presumably still fragile.

And while riders regularly return from broken collarbones within weeks, Pogačar would lose a valuable, rare opportunity to fully unplug and recharge for 2027 if he starts the hilly 196km champs.

He loves to race, and he’s got clear motivation to rush back to the bike and please his home crowds.

Or who knows? Maybe he just really dislikes his UAE Emirates-XRG trade team jersey.

He’ll be wearing it for the first time in two years next season if he doesn’t win the blue and white European top on Sunday.

American Brandon McNulty celebrates after winning the elite men Road Race race (273,7 km) at the cycling World Championship, in Montreal, Canada, Sunday 27 September 2026. The UCI road world championships are taking place from 20 to 27 September, in Montreal, Canada. BELGA PHOTO JASPER JACOBS (Photo by JASPER JACOBS / BELGA MAG / Belga / AFP via Getty Images) (Photo: JASPER JACOBS / BELGA MAG / Belga / AFP via Getty Images)

When I wrote a preview article that named Brandon McNulty as one of the favorites for the UCI Road World Championships in Montreal, I didn’t think it was actually possible. Of course, McNulty was a previous winner of the GP Montreal, as well as a rider in form who had just finished fourth in the Worlds time trial. But he would have to beat the likes of Remco Evenepoel, Mathieu van der Poel, Wout van Aert, Isaac del Toro, Paul Seixas, and so many other riders. An American hadn’t won the World Championships since 1993, and McNulty hadn’t won a race in the entire 2026 season.

But when Team USA showed up with the strongest riders in the race, it was only a matter of time until one of those was soloing to victory. First, Quinn Simmons gave it a crack. Then, it was Matteo Jorgenson closing down key attacks. And finally, it was McNulty’s turn to go. The 28-year-old went solo with 32km to go, and held on to win by only 13 seconds ahead of Michael Matthews and Van der Poel.

This is how Brandon McNulty won the World Championships Road Race.

Before the start of the 2026 Road World Championships, there was a lot of talk about the course that resembled the Grand Prix Cycliste de Montréal. The World Championships used almost the exact same city circuits as the Canadian classic, including the Voie Camillien-Houde, a four-minute climb with an average gradient of 7.9%.

The GP Montreal included 16 laps of the city circuits and Voie Camillien-Houde, while the World Championships only included 12. Instead of additional laps, the Worlds RR added 100 kilometers of flat road to bring the total race distance to 273.4km. This makes a physiological analysis of the race a bit deceiving because the average effort of the race is not a true representation of what actually happened.

Quinn Simmons, for example, went on to finish 4th with an average power of 298w (NP 379w) for six hours and 17 minutes. However, Simmons only averaged 204w for the first 100km of the race, and 346w (NP 415w) for the last 173km. For the rest of this article, we are going to focus on the second part of the race — the hard part — once the peloton enters the Montreal city circuits. While the first 100km cannot be discounted, it’s unlikely that they added a significant amount of fatigue to any of the favorites’ legs.

The race truly began when Bruno Amirail went to the front of the peloton and started smashing the peloton to bits. Amirail averaged more than 400w for 90 minutes, with a Normalized Power of 440w on the hilly city circuit. He even pushed the lap button on his headunit, knowing he was about to do a 90-minute time trial.

In hindsight, Amirail did way too much way too early. What was the point of this massive pull? Amirail closed down the early breakaway, but that group never had a chance of making it to the finish anyway. The Frenchman didn’t set up an attack either. In fact, he rode so hard that the rest of the French team was fairly useless for the rest of the race. Their chosen leader, Paul Seixas, would cramp out of the chase group in the finale.

Amirail’s numbers are certainly impressive, but it’s the perfect example of wasting watts in a race that would reward tactics over pure strength.

Over the next two hours, there were countless attacks from the pre-race favorites, and soon there was a group that managed to slip away. With 80km to go, a leading group of six had formed that contained Van der Poel, Van Aert, and Simmons. This was about to be a turning point in the race, and just before the peloton hit the Voie Camillien-Houde, Pidcock was forced to chase back after a mishap.

Del Toro attacked halfway up the climb with Evenepoel, Seixas, and McNulty on his wheel. The Mexican kept pushing while Ben Healy and a handful of others were struggling to hold the wheel. Only 10 riders made it over the top of the climb on the wheel of Del Toro, who had just done the fastest ascent of the Voie Camillien-Houde in the entire race. Healy was one of the select few to make the split, and we can see that the Irishman pushed nearly 8w/kg for four minutes.

Healy – Voie Camillien-Houde with 78km to go

Following Del Toro’s attack, there was a lull in the chase group that allowed a number of riders to catch back on. Meanwhile, the lead group was split by an attack from Van der Poel, who was only followed by Simmons and Oscar Onley. If you’ve ever wondered what it takes to follow an attack from Mathieu van der Poel, look no further than Simmons’ power file: 880w for 26 seconds with a peak power of 1,093w.

Attacks continued to fly for the next hour, and this is when we saw the first cracks in the pre-race favorites. Evenepoel was getting dropped every few minutes, as well as Mauro Schmid, Van Aert, and Mads Pedersen. The Dane was so far behind that we didn’t even see him until the finale…he would go on to finish sixth.

With 36km to go, McNulty and Del Toro were chatting at the back of the chase group after the Mexican had just attacked. We don’t know what was said, but 6km later, McNulty attacked while Del Toro was on the front of the group. No one reacted, and the American quickly built a 30-second lead over the next few kilometers.

The key to understanding the rest of this race lies in the reality of fatigue resistance. For the final 32km of the World Championships, every rider went slower and slower. McNulty said he was pushing Zone 2 pace up the final climb, and we’ll look at those numbers in a minute. No one was setting power PRs on the final lap. In fact, most of them were crawling to the finish.…

When Brandon McNulty rolled across the line to win the 2026 UCI Road World Championships , it marked the end of a journey. Over the past decade, the United States men’s riders have been building momentum.

It started slowly at first, with promising results like McNulty winning bronze in the junior time trial at Richmond in 2015, and then accelerated with Quinn Simmons’ junior worlds road race title in 2019, Sepp Kuss winning the Vuelta a España in 2023 and Matteo Jorgenson taking back to back titles at Paris-Nice in 2024 and 2025.

Yet, the rainbow jersey that McNulty will take into 2027 is a whole different milestone. The U.S’s last men’s elite world championship was 33 years ago, when 21-year-old Lance Armstrong won in Oslo. The only other American man to wear the rainbow jersey before that was Greg LeMond.

“I’ve been in the USAC organization since I was 16 years old,” McNulty said after the race. “I was a child when I first met a lot of the people that are still involved in the organization. I’ve been to almost every World Championships since then.

“I was able to win the TT as a junior at the 2016 worlds, and then Quinn Simmons won the junior road race a few years later, so there’s been success. But I think the men’s road race has always been the dream for everyone in the organization. It’s super special to do with people that I’ve known since I was really a kid.”

McNulty is the leader of this generation that has elevated American cycling to near the top of the world rankings. While Sepp Kuss and Neilson Powless are both older and winners on the WorldTour level, McNulty was so talented as a junior that he became a model for what Americans could do starting at this younger level.

Both Kuss and Powless really found their success at cycling’s top level gradually as established professionals rather than from the jump as development projects. McNulty was different. At just 17, he was not only already racing in Europe, but he was also strong enough of a time trialist to set a course record at pro-level races in the United States—on junior gears. He was about as hyped as a junior cyclist could be.

It was during those junior years that the rest of the core of this generation also started to elevate their level. Matteo Jorgenson, who is a year younger than McNulty, is a key example of this.

When they raced in America, the two were rivals, as McNulty was the best rider on the Lux Cycling Team and Jorgenson was the top rider at Hot Tubes. Yet, in the summer, the two would come together for long European race blocks where they learned to race together as much as they competed against one another.

“I started racing with USA Cycling in Belgium when I was 16, just doing Kermesses for three weeks,” McNulty said of his time in the junior ranks. “At the time, it was a dream to be a pro, but you have no idea what that would have meant.

“I found success which, at the time, felt huge. Winning in Europe as an American felt crazy, so that confidence was the foundation. It’s special because Matteo [Jorgenson] was also on that trip. To know we’ve been doing this together for that long…it’s cool to grow up like that all together.”

That dynamic, the very friendly rivalry, started what effectively became a chain of talent. The mix of the US Junior National Team and the two dominant junior teams kept putting the most talented riders in scenarios of competition and collaboration. It was McNulty racing Jorgenson; then it was Jorgenson racing Sean Quinn, Kevin Vermaerke, and Riley Sheehan; and so on and so forth. That chain extends all the way to Ashlin Barry, who managed to do something that McNulty, Jorgenson, or Simmons couldn’t when he won America’s first U23 World Championship on Friday.

Altogether, it was that collective energy that built through the years that cemented the victory in Montreal. It was the interwoven story of those riders working to make the big junior teams, to beat out other juniors for the national team race blocks, and to work together to challenge European talent on their home turf. All of that set the table for the team performance that was remarkably cohesive for a national team performance.

“I think those guys were really lucky that in their junior and under-23 careers they got to be a part of those teams,” Michael Creed, the DS for the US team, told Velo about the power of the development structure that the US team created. “I run a devo team, so I know and appreciate what they do, because I know how hard it can be.”

According to Creed, that challenge—that grind—could have a direct relationship to the way they raced together when it mattered most.

“They raced like the US has won the world championship a lot of times, but maybe they raced that way because they knew how rare it was.”

Ultimately, the United States has always had riders capable of a top result in certain races. Before this generation, there was a strong cohort of riders like Tejay van Garderen, Ian Boswell, Ben King, and Taylor Phinney.

Yet, even with their success, having three Americans in the top 10 at Worlds, let alone winning the race, has never happened.

“There was a fundamental change in the psyche of American cyclists,” Boswell told Velo after the race. “My generation was very influenced by the previous generation. Almost every rider was a kind of GC type stage racer.

“That’s all what we wanted to be because that’s what we saw ahead of us. This generation hasn’t put themselves in that same box.”

For riders like Boswell, the inspiration was the likes of Lance Armstrong, Tyler Hamilton, and Levi Leipheimer. With that kind of legacy, and with the reckoning from the fallout of that generation’s doping hitting home after those riders already were well on their way to professional careers, that line of thinking makes sense.…

Demi Vollering (Netherlands) wins the European road championships on October 03, 2026 in Sencur, Slovenia. (Photo: Szymon Gruchalski/Getty Images) (Photo: Szymon Gruchalski)

One week after becoming world champion for the first time, Demi Vollering has doubled up with the European champs jersey, successfully defending the title she won last year.

Vollering continued a dream season with an assertive solo performance, going clear on the final lap with worlds runner-up Kasia Niewiadoma (Poland) and her own Dutch teammate Puck Pieterse. They dropped the other favorites on the Možjanca climb, with Vollering then kicking clear alone with just under 15km remaining.

Niewiadoma chased hard but with Pieterse sitting on, the duo were 34 seconds back with 12.2km to go. They were joined by Elisa Longo Borghini (Italy) and Antonia Niedermaier (Germany), with Marlen Reusser (Switzerland) bridging soon afterwards.

That gave the chasers numerical advantage but Vollering was too powerful, driving onwards towards the finish and notching up yet another win in what is a stunning season.

“It is really a golden year,” she said. “It is sad it is already over. Only the TT, and then it is off season already. But I cannot wait to race next year all year in this jersey and hopefully have a good season again.”

Niewiadoma crashed towards the finish, losing any chance of a medal. Pieterse won the sprint for second, five seconds back, with Reusser and Longo Borghini third and fourth. Niedermaier was 15 seconds adrift while a disappointed Niewiadoma limped in 45 seconds behind.

She will rue losing the chance to go for a medal, but Vollering was clearly a class above everyone.

“I just really love winning and it never gets boring for me,” she said, making clear that she still has many dreams in the sport.

“I think also it is not only the winning for me, but just proving yourself and getting better every day. Working on yourself every day and seeing what is still possible for the future. I think that is what I love most about this job.”

The elite women’s road race had a very different course to that of last week’s world road championship. The course in Montréal was very draining but Saturday’s 130km event in Slovenia was primarily flat for the first two thirds. However, following the start of two finishing laps, things did get more difficult.

The riders would face the Možjanca climb on each of those laps and while it was just 2.1km in length, it averaged 10.4 percent.

The days break saw Carina Schrempf (Austria) and Margot Vanpachtenbeke (Belgium) go clear less than 10km from the start and remain out front until 39km to go. The first ascent of the climb saw Reusser surge with 35km to go and force a group clear containing the world champion Vollering, Pieterse, Longo Borghini, Niedermaier, Niewiadoma and Juliette Berthet (France).

However while these are all very powerful riders, the terrain enabled a large regrouping on and after the descent.

Franziska Koch (Germany) and Cecilie Uttrup Ludwig (Denmark) then played their hand with 28km remaining. They got 25 seconds but were gobbled up with 19km left, just before Liane Lippert (Germany) attacked on a ramp and was joined by Noemi Rüegg (Switzerland) and Femke De Vries (Netherlands).

That trio sped towards the climb with a lead of 20 seconds but were reeled in with 16km remaining. Vollering, Pieterse and Niewiadoma pushed forward on the uphill but when the world champion surged with just under 15km remaining, she quickly moved clear.

Niewiadoma chased, with Pieterse sitting on, and while Longo Borghini, Niedermaier and Reusser rejoined, that collective strength could do nothing against Vollering.

She was well able to hold them off, racing to her second major triumph in eight days.

Does your daily diet properly support your cycling training and recovery?

Are you getting enough carbs to sustain your biggest rides? But what about when you’re slaving at the 9-to-5?

What about protein – how much should cyclists really be getting?

And honestly, do you need that shelf of a dozen different supplements?

All these questions – and many more – have been answered by 52 of the world’s leading sport and nutrition scientists in a newly published “ Position Statement on Nutrition for Cycling .”

The weighty 18,000-word tome tells you everything you could possibly want to know about nutrition, on and off the bike.

It speaks to training, recovery, illness, female health, training at altitude … everything.

Big brains from WorldTour superteams, national federations, and research laboratories collaborated on the authorship. The UCI commissioned and rubber-stamped it.

There’s no bro science or social media “fact” here.

The paper is an epic encyclopedia of information for hard-training amateurs who balance biking ambitions with pesky real life. And we read every single word of it, so you don’t have to.

To give you the ultimate guide to dialing in your diet for training, recovery, and health.

What follows is based on information directly from the UCI bible, supported by Velo ‘s own research and calls with pro cycling team staff.

Note that we haven’t included on-bike nutrition or performance supplements here. Those are very deep rabbit holes that require separate exploration.

In the meantime, here are Velo’s guides on supplements and fueling .

And before we start: One important caveat.

There is no such thing as a “perfect” diet. Don’t get bogged down tracking calories and measuring skin folds. Use your health, happiness, and trends in blood markers, body mass, and power output as your guiding stars.

Take the below as guiding principles, not strict “rules.”

Overall intake and energy availability is the base of the nutritional pyramid. There’s no point finessing macro- and micro- nutrients if these are out of line.

The UCI paper recommends that daily energy availability should be 40 to 45 calories per kilo of fat-free mass, per day.

This calculation gives athletes a good ballpark figure for how many calories riders should eat every day, according to their training volume.

Don’t worry, basically nobody outside the sporting elite knows theirs either. We’ve laid out in the appendix below how you can calculate your own fat-free mass.

However, the UCI’s basic message regarding energy availability is that cyclists need to eat enough, all the time. Otherwise, all that training is a waste of time.

And trust us, you probably need significantly more food than you think. Run the numbers through the energy availability equation below, and you’ll be surprised.

1. The UCI paper is keen to enforce that lighter is not always better. That stance reflects how the WorldTour is increasingly focusing on power before weight in its quest to optimize the watts-per-kilo equation.

Amateurs should follow suit. Health and power output should be prioritized before any weight loss goals, unless medically advised.

2. Short periods of low energy availability (LEA) are “unlikely to be problematic” if the athlete allows full recovery time, and doesn’t fall into LEA regularly. However, prolonged LEA, or repeat bouts of short-term LEA, leaves athletes flirting with relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S).

Athletes need to pay particular attention to pre- and post-ride nutrition to safeguard against this damaging condition.

3. For female athletes: There are currently no generalized recommendations for how to alter dietary intake around hormonal fluctuations. The current consensus is that athletes track their cycles and adjust nutrition based on their personal experience and symptoms.

Carbohydrates must be the foundation of any athlete’s food plan. Forget the fad for Atkins and carnivore diets, and turn down the pre-pandemic hype for low-carb training.

Carbohydrates fuel the engine, support muscular repair, and play a crucial role in bone metabolism and immune function.

Carbs should be up- and down-scaled according to training.

Remember the saying “fuel for the work required”? Exactly.

The UCI provided useful daily carbohydrate targets for athletes at four activity levels.

We worked the recommendations through some example athletes to give you a quick guide.

1. The guidance above includes all the crap you eat on the bike. So, a 70kg rider who trained for more than four hours should include the glut of candies, gels, and café stop cookies in their recommended total of 560 grams of carbohydrate.

2. Carbohydrate targets look different for riders who are “carb loading” ahead of a big race or fondo. In those cases, athletes should eat 10 to 12g carbohydrate per day for two days before rollout. And this time, that’s on top of any carbs eaten in training on those days.

3. Prioritize carbohydrates in the immediate post-workout daze. Glycogen replenishment should be considered the first priority, with protein – contrary to popular belief – being second.

Target 1-1.2 grams of carbs per kilo of bodyweight within the first hour of training, and continue carbing at that rate for 3 to 4 hours thereafter.

4. The UCI’s panel of experts advises caution over “fasted” training. Training on empty should be applied strategically and sparingly, and shouldn’t be seen as a route toward body composition goals. Athletes should ensure full energy availability at the end of a day of lower-carb training.

Cyclists should eat protein like they’re bodybuilders . That is, they need a lot of it, spread relatively evenly throughout the day.

Protein supports repair and regrowth. Athletes can’t progress without it, whether they want to bench press 200 kilos or ride 200 miles of Kansan gravel. And for higher-volume riders, protein is crucial for protecting against muscle wastage.…

Brandon McNulty is a unique rider in more ways than one. Not only did he become the first American to win the elite road race at the 2026 UCI Road World Championships in more than 30 years, but he is also a rider who never goes to altitude camps. The Arizonan rides alongside Tadej Pogačar at the Tour de France, but instead of living on a mountain a month before the Tour, he is more often at home, training at 5:00 a.m. in the desert.

When McNulty lined up for the World Championships in Montreal, many considered him an outsider with a chance at a medal, but few thought that he had the capacity to win. The 28-year-old hadn’t won a race in the entire 2026 season, which was quite concerning after he rounded out the 2025 season by winning six races in two months, including the WorldTour-level Tour de Pologne and Grand Prix Cycliste de Montréal.

Whatever happened in the 2025/2026 off-season remains a bit of a mystery, yet McNulty started the year with a few top-five finishes in February. After a DNF at Paris-Nice, McNulty was solid again in April before taking a short break pre-Tour de Suisse. The American showed good form while helping Pogačar, but he was still never in the top five throughout the entire race. His best finish at the Tour was fifth place on a breakaway stage, and the rest of his time in France was spent helping Pogačar.

McNulty’s results were nothing to write home about, so few considered him as a worlds favorite. But between his DNF on Stage 18 of the Tour de France on July 23 and winning the World Championships on September 27, something changed. This is how Brandon McNulty trained to win the rainbow jersey.

There were exactly 66 days between July 23 and September 27, which means that McNulty had nine and a half weeks to go from abandoning the Tour to winning worlds. First, he took 10 days off the bike. That is a long break in the middle of the season, but in hindsight, it was the perfect amount of time. McNulty then returned to training with five consecutive easy rides — that means Zone 1 and Zone 2, without intervals or any additional stress. He was riding 2-3 hours a day, not the 5-6 daily hours that you might expect from other professional cyclists.

His first workout post-Tour de France was a classic UAE Team Emirates session: four-minute torque intervals. We’ll see these a lot in McNulty’s training plan, and they are much harder than they look. In this post-Tour workout, McNulty did 7x4min at 45 rpm, getting up to a max heart rate of ~170 bpm at the end of each interval. Knowing McNulty’s heart rate zones and history, we can assume these intervals were done at threshold power, which is likely around 450w for McNulty.

Workout #1: 4-minute torque intervals (45 rpm) at 100% FTP

The day after this torque workout, McNulty completed 3x30min intervals with a heart rate of 155-165bpm during each 30min block. That means he was probably riding at Tempo, or Zone 3. McNulty said that he climbed the Voie Camillien-Houde in Zone 2 on the final lap of the World Championships, and by my calculations, McNulty’s Zone 2 is approximately 5.3w/kg, or 365w. That means these Tempo intervals are likely done at 380-400w, making for an interval session like this isn’t the toughest, but it’s crucial to get accustomed to riding at this pace for extended periods of time, especially when you are training to win races solo.

One of the key principles of McNulty’s training plan is progressive overload, and that’s exactly what we saw with his first ride five weeks out from worlds. The American did 3x35min Tempo at 145-155 bpm, up from 3x30min the week before. The same principle applies to the short torque intervals, which now added a 30-second sprint at the end of each interval. McNulty also completed an additional rep, which meant this week’s workout was 8x4min Torque intervals (45 rpm) at 100% FTP straight into a 30-second sprint.

After a few days of Zone 2 and recovery riding, McNulty went out for a two-hour endurance ride on Friday, but this one was different. Twenty minutes after he got home, McNulty was on the trainer for an hour with his heart rate rising from 130 bpm to 170 bpm by the end of the session. It’s extremely likely that this was a heat training session, something that McNulty and so many other pros have been utilizing before key races each season. The following day included the same style of Tempo intervals that we’ve already seen, but this time they were 40 minutes each.

The following day included a new workout in this block of training: 3x10min 30/30s from 160-170 bpm. Since McNulty is only hitting 90% of his max heart rate, my best guess is that these 30/30s are done just below and just above threshold. For McNulty, this could be something like: 30 seconds at 420w followed by 30 seconds at 470w.

Next up was another threshold interval session, but this time with much longer blocks. This workout was 2x20min over/unders with one minute VO2 Max followed by four minutes just under threshold. Intervals like these are designed to train your body to clear lactate, even at a high power output. The days of 2x20min at FTP are gone; almost every modern-day pro is doing over/unders instead.

At the end of this training week, McNulty did his worlds prep session: 6x4min VO2 Max and 6x30sec sprints. This is an incredibly hard workout, but one that McNulty uses to get into race shape. Not only are the VO2 Max intervals challenging, but the sheer number of efforts in this workout is a true challenge of fatigue resistance. Doing a fresh 30-second sprint is one thing; now try doing 30 seconds all-out after spending 24 minutes in your VO2 Max zone and sprinting five times full gas. These are the kinds of workouts that give McNulty the ability to attack four hours deep into a hard race.…

An industrial nightmare was brewing south of Los Angeles.

In late May, a chemical storage tank with more than 7,000 gallons of toxic material began heating up – fast. The tank belonged to GKN Aerospace, a company that supplies parts to the aviation industry, including aircraft windows.

As the temperature inside the shiny metal storage vessel rose, workers realised they had a problem. The tank was at risk of exploding, potentially showering nearby neighbourhoods with methyl methacrylate (MMA), a skin and lung-irritating , external compound used in plastics production.

The tank's temperature reached 100F (38C) – though possibly went higher - 100F was simply the maximum reading , external on the temperature gauge inside.

More than 50,000 residents of Garden Grove city were evacuated and fire crews began hosing down the tank in a bid to cool it. At one point, the vessel "actually bulged" according to the local fire chief.

Thankfully, no explosion occurred. Months later, in August, GKN and local authorities announced a $100m (£74m) programme , external to compensate residents evacuated during the incident. But production of aircraft windows at the site, which had been halted, is still not fully restored.

This has sent a minor shockwave through the aircraft manufacturing industry because GKN is one of surprisingly few companies, anywhere in the world, that make aircraft windows – highly engineered, safety-critical parts for planes.

Production at GKN's Garden Grove facility currently remains hobbled, at roughly 50% of normal, according to public statements , external by its UK parent company Melrose Industries. The aim is to have full production restored by 28 September. GKN declined an interview with the BBC.

"They're one of only a handful of suppliers – less than a handful, really – of critical windows," says Marisa Garcia, an aviation industry analyst. "One of the breaking points of supply chain in aviation is you have very few companies qualified to do something and, when something goes wrong, it really upsets the entire system."

Boeing tells the BBC it is "taking steps to mitigate any potential impacts", describing the shortfall in production as an "industry-wide" situation.

"We are supporting our supplier," a spokesman adds. An Airbus spokeswoman says, "We are closely monitoring and are seeing positive progress toward a return to normal."

It comes at a time when airlines "can't get new aircraft fast enough," says Mike Stengel of AeroDynamic Advisory, a consultancy. "They're holding on to aircraft for longer."

Even though there are just a few aircraft window-manufacturing firms in existence, it's hard for new competitors to emerge because of how regulated the industry is, adds Stengel. "It can take time to pivot to a new supplier."

This leads to a "balancing act" between plane-makers and the firms they rely on for various parts, Stengel says.

To find out what goes into the making of an aircraft window, I spoke to Jean-Eric Vermont, general manager of French company Saint-Gobain Aerospace.

"We focus mostly on commercial aircraft, regional aircraft and helicopters," he says. Vermont declines, though, to say how much market share his company has in aircraft windows – or transparencies, as they are known in the trade.

The oval-shaped windows in the cabin, next to passengers' seats, are typically made of plastic-based materials, says Vermont. "You start from a sheet of acrylic," he explains. "Then you cut to size, [to] give the shape."

A Saint-Gobain spokesman confirmed to the BBC that the company does not store or process MMA like GKN, but rather purchases sheets of polymerised MMA, or acrylic.

Aircraft manufacturers are increasingly ordering larger cabin windows, says Vermont, in order to offer passengers a wider view of the world outside. It's a selling point but it requires additional testing to ascertain whether the bigger windows hold up as well as the smaller ones.

Saint-Gobain tests its windows by exposing them to pressures many times what would be normal on an aircraft flying at altitude.

These acrylic-based cabin windows are usually made out of two layers or plies, and Saint-Gobain also performs tests to confirm whether the window will survive even if one of those plies gets damaged.

Cockpit windows, Vermont says, are "totally different".

They are generally made of glass, which is chemically reinforced by adding potassium to it. This involves swapping smaller sodium ions for larger potassium ions, which helps to fill out the molecular structure of the glass, meaning that when it cools during production, it compresses into an extra strong, tight formation as it cools.

Some of the latest aircraft feature cockpit windows that are also curved, to make the plane more streamlined, which improves fuel efficiency. But curved cockpit windows are challenging to make – the slightest distortion or defect is clearly visible to the pilot.

Quality control checks are used to ensure no such impediments exist in the final product.

All aircraft windows must be resistant to impacts but cockpit windows, at the front of the plane, are especially vulnerable to bird strikes, says Vermont: "The issue is not the speed of the bird, the issue is the speed of the aircraft."

Saint-Gobain uses numerical simulations and "physical tests representative of a sizeable bird impact" to test its windows against this threat.

"Typically, if you go through a hailstorm or if you hit a large enough bird, the external ply will crack," says Vermont. "The cockpit window is designed for that."

A London to Londonderry flight was recently affected by a cracked cockpit window . While a mid-air emergency was declared, the plane landed safely. "There can be [such] cases," says Vermont, though he adds that Saint-Gobain's windows have not been involved in any recently.…

It's in Duncan Trevithick's interest to be good at using AI at work - if he can use it to get more tasks done, faster, he'll qualify for a bonus at the end of the year.

On the surface, it's a great incentive. But he's questioning what's really in it for him.

"The uncomfortable interpretation is that employees are being assessed on how effectively they can participate in their own redundancy," says Spain-based Trevithick, 34, who works in marketing for an AI training data company.

But if he uses AI to take care of two days worth of work each week, he says the financial rewards don't add up.

"I do not receive two days off or a 40% pay rise. The higher output simply becomes the new baseline. In the short term, that may help me get promoted. In the longer term, I have helped prove how much of my job no longer requires me," he says.

"I'm just trying to view myself as a manager, and I'm managing some people, and I'm also managing AI agents, or AI loops, or whatever you want to call it."

Using employees' AI abilities as a measure of whether they should get a bonus, promoted - or even sacked - is fast becoming more common.

Accenture CEO Julie Sweet told the Rapid Response podcast in March: "Today, AI at Accenture is how we do work. So if you want to get promoted, you've got to do the things that we do in order to operate at Accenture."

And big names like Disney, Meta, JP Morgan and KPMG have introduced "AI leaderboards" to track and rank employees' usage of the array of LLMs and platforms at their disposal, according to media reports , external . Crypto trading platform Coinbase has already fired engineers who didn't complete AI training, as requested by the chief executive, Brian Armstrong , external .

It demonstrates how eager business leaders are to see a return from their AI investments, especially when 94% of companies have yet to see significant value from AI, according to a report , external by consultants McKinsey.

Employees feel they have to get on board, thanks to the current state of the jobs market - in the UK, vacancies have hit a five-year low .

Meanwhile, 75% of the 1,881 UK jobseekers polled in July by recruiter Gi Group say they would not be put off applying to an organisation that had introduced AI proficiency into individual performance reviews. Around 22% said it would be off-putting.

"It's like being in the sea and you see a giant wave coming. You can get out a surfboard and try and ride it as long as possible, or you can just let it take you under. But you can't stop the wave," says Trevithick.

But what's going on at the large consultancy Pamela (her name has been changed to protect her identity) works for isn't sitting right with her.

She's a US-based senior executive who has observed that, while there isn't a formal mandate for employees to use AI, it's obviously determining who is rewarded, and who is left behind.

"The ground is shifting under us. You've got to demonstrate [AI] fluency and fluidity as one of your key achievements. It's kind of quiet where nobody's saying, 'learn AI or else'. But let me tell you, in performance reviews, they reward who uses it well," says Pamela.

That shift, she adds, means that AI capabilities are now counting for more than actual experience, which is creating a "two tier workforce".

"You've got the same job title, same tenure, but different value based on whether someone treats AI as a threat or a tool - that gap widens really quickly once leadership notices it," says Pamela.

"AI fluency beats credentials every day. Somebody that has 15, 20 years of experience and no AI fluency will be passed over for those that have, say, three years, but are fast with the tools."

She adds: "If you're not visibly using AI, you see slower promotion timelines. It's harder to be seen, and it's harder to fight being on that shortlist."

But is it legal for companies to shift the goal posts like this?

Legally, bosses are in the clear, confirms Tina Chander, partner and employment lawyer at Weightmans. But she says it does open up questions about pay and fairness.

"The question then becomes whether the employer increases expectations on the basis that the employee can now produce more work. Is that fair?" questions Chander.

"And if an employee is effectively doing more because AI has made them more efficient, should they be rewarded differently? Or are they effectively making themselves redundant, thus acting as a disincentive to be productive?"

Chander advises businesses to have clear policies, training and boundaries in place, otherwise they risk employees opening up disputes about fairness, performance expectations and job security.

Indeed, from January 2027, UK employees will have six months to submit unfair dismissal claims compared with the current three months, and will be able to do so after just six months service , rather than the current two years.

Yet HR consultant Tina Rahman says employers aren't currently being transparent enough in telling employees why they want AI to be part of people's jobs, and what the end purpose of that is - which she agrees is to save costs and time, but also to cut down on outsourcing.

"Because they misunderstand it, this is not being reflected to employees," says Rahman, who runs a London-based consultancy, HR Habitat.

A lack of clarity around AI usage is certainly causing discontent at Pamela's company.

"Leadership is being inconsistent and vague on purpose. Firms want productivity gains without owning the disruption narrative," she says.

"If something goes wrong, they're going to say, 'I didn't tell you to do that. Where'd you get that from?' Then if you did something with AI, and it works, great."

Mandating AI use at work can become purely performative, rather than having any real positive impact, warns Kamila Miller, applied AI researcher and lecturer at Henley Business School.…

The price of diesel in the UK has breached the £2 per litre mark for the first time, as the fallout from the US-Israel war with Iran continues to drive up costs.

The average price of a litre of diesel at the pump stands at an all-time high of 200.01p, according to the RAC motoring body.

Over the past seven months, the Iran war has severely disrupted the production and transportation of oil across the region, causing the price of fuels made from crude to surge.

Motor fuel prices fell back when the US and Iran agreed in June to a framework deal to end the fighting, but rose again as tensions resurfaced.

Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump has responded to rising prices by mulling a ban on US diesel producers selling overseas - a move which could push UK prices even higher.

Crude oil is a key ingredient in petrol and diesel, which means that higher wholesale costs make filling up a car more expensive. The price of petrol and diesel is also heavily influenced by demand and refining capacity.

Analysts say every $10 (£7.55) per barrel increase in the oil price pushes up pump prices by roughly 7p a litre.

Since the Iran war began, the price of a barrel of Brent crude – the global benchmark for wholesale oil prices – has been very volatile.

Generally speaking, news of further conflict drives the price up while hopes of an end to the war pushes the price down.

Before the Middle East conflict, Brent was trading just over $70 a barrel but the fighting saw it peak at above $120.

In early July, after the framework deal was signed, prices fell back to near the $70 mark.

The price climbed back up again after peace talks collapsed and it is now around $100 a barrel.

A lot of oil is produced in the Middle East, and the conflict has severely disrupted the production and the transportation of it, causing its price to jump.

Of particular concern to wholesale oil traders was Iran's effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz - a vital waterway south of the country through which one fifth of the world's oil and gas usually flows.

There are signs that wholesale oil transport through the strait is returning to pre-war levels, but wholesale prices remain high because traders fear this might not last.

Meanwhile, the transportation of refined oil products, such as car and plane fuel, remains down because of damage to refineries in the region and because refined products are more flammable, making them more dangerous to move during a conflict.

Before the war began, the average price of petrol was 132.83p per litre and diesel was 142.38p, according to the RAC.

Diesel is now 200.01p, the highest on record.

Meanwhile, petrol has hit an average 174.71p a litre, which is the highest in more than four years but lower than its peak of 191.5p during the summer of 2022.

Simon Williams, head of policy at the RAC, said prices at the pumps will not come down until there is a "sustained lower oil price - over several weeks, not days".

Because transporting oil is a slow process, price movements in wholesale oil markets take about a fortnight to show at the pump.

Fuel retailers have denied accusations of price gouging during the conflict. The official markets regulator said it had "not seen evidence of retailers actively changing their pricing strategies to take advantage of the crisis".

A government scheme called Fuel Finder , external lets drivers compare the cost of fuel offered by petrol stations across the UK.

In May, the then Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer said a planned 5p increase in fuel duty due in September would be postponed until the end of December because of the conflict.

Williams said that the UK government has "limited leverage when it comes to ending the US/Iran war" but lowering fuel duty further or reducing VAT could "ease the burden" at home.

Even if you don't drive a diesel car, you could still be hit by the rise in diesel prices.

That's because diesel is used heavily in agriculture and, crucially, in haulage.

So transporting some of our biggest essentials – particularly food – around the country is getting more expensive.

Previous episodes of high costs at the pumps have even had a knock-on effect on school transport and trips, putting pressure on councils and schools, particularly in rural areas.

No evidence of widespread fuel price-gouging, watchdog says

Drivers can compare fuel prices at different petrol stations - how does it work?

While Trump has suggested he might ban US producers from selling diesel overseas, he has not done it yet and views differ on how serious this threat is.

If it does happen, many agree it would hurt the countries which heavily depend on US diesel.

One such country is the UK, which depends on the US for around 17% of its diesel supplies. Other European countries also import a lot of US diesel.

As such, many worry any ban could drive UK diesel prices up even further.

And while the ban would be likely to reduce US diesel prices in the short-term, experts say it could have unintended effects that could hurt US production – and put pressure on US diesel prices – in the long-term.

In the UK, we have four refineries. Between them, they make more than enough petrol to meet our needs, so we sell the rest as export.

However, they don't make enough diesel, which means we rely on imports. The closure last year of refineries in Grangemouth and Immingham has increased that reliance, meaning we now buy over half of our diesel from overseas.

In addition, the cost of importing diesel has risen because of Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Although the UK has stopped buying Russian diesel in response to the war, other countries have carried on, meaning you have "more countries competing for less diesel", the RAC's Williams says.

All of this then feeds through to prices at the pump, with diesel costing much more than petrol in the UK and the gap having widened over the last few years.…

Households across Northern Ireland face increasing pressure on the cost of living as energy price hikes have come into effect.

Northern Ireland's largest provider of natural gas, SSE Airtricity, increased its prices by almost 19% on Thursday for its 200,000 domestic and small business customers.

That means the annual gas bill of a typical household in the greater Belfast and west gas network areas will increase by almost £172.

The company said "unprecedented levels of volatility in global energy markets and higher wholesale gas prices" had led to the price rise.

Wholesale gas prices in the UK have effectively doubled since the US and Israel began their attack on Iran.

Keeping the house warm is particularly important for parents with young children and babies.

Lucy Kells is a mum of two in east Belfast on maternity leave.

She said she expects the winter months to be difficult because "most people are going to have to have the heating on, especially if you've young kids in the house".

"There's no escaping it - everything feels more expensive and it is more expensive."

She added that, despite "budgeting proactively" and "being as careful as you can with savings and credit cards", rising bills mean people's financial situations are out of their control.

"You have to cut somewhere else and I already feel we are doing that," she said.

Lucy is one of the parents who attends a weekly baby class at Woodstock Library in east Belfast.

Branch manager Nuala Hyde said she has noticed more people using their free activities to combat the rising cost of living.

She said: "As well as families, we have lots of older people coming in now to keep warm."

"We have people coming in who will stay all day, use the computer, have a chat and stay until closing time sometimes, so it is quite evident that we are providing an essential service at the minute when people are struggling," she added.

Ryan McStay is a final year student at St Mary's University College Belfast, where he is studying to become a primary school teacher.

"Somebody is already struggling with the fact that they're dying. To then know that they can't keep their house warm."

Naomi explained that a number of factors contribute to the increased energy needs, including the need to stay warm, different sleeping patterns, and essential medical devices.

She said some patients have turned down services that could help improve their quality of life because they can't pay their electricity bills.

Naomi said terminal illness adds further costs for patients, such as the cost of transport to and from hospital appointments.

"There is a huge problem, and you see that struggle often.

"I'm really saddened. The support is limited, there is very little out there. There is no reduction in costs of their electricity, even though their needs are so much higher and essential for their care."

Naomi added that Marie Curie have called for the implementation of a "social tariff" for people with terminal illnesses, to ease their financial burden.

"It would make such a huge difference to have that bit of extra money in your last months of life, so you're comfortable and you can spend it with your family," she said.

She said some people spend the end of their life working because they "don't have any other access to money".

"You end up dying not being able to keep your house warm. That to me is just devastating."

The US is a vital supplier of diesel to the world, exporting between 1.2 and 1.5 million barrels per day, with experts warning a ban on shipments abroad could put further pressure on prices in other countries.

"We're thinking about it very seriously," Trump said of an export ban at the weekend.

Energy Minister Martin McCluskey was on a call with European counterparts on Thursday to discuss the potential ban.

A source familiar with the discussions told the BBC it was prudent to prepare a co-ordinated response with other countries, including those across EU, but added that there were still European reserves left from a coordinated release of strategic fuel stocks earlier in the year.

"We have a diverse and resilient supply. We continue to engage with our international partners and the UK fuel industry," a government spokesperson said. The government has stressed that there is no cause for concern about potential diesel shortages, though prices are expected to rise further.

What a US diesel export ban could mean for you

A European Commission spokesperson said today that there were "lots of calls, lots of meetings" taking place on the diesel situation, including with "high level contacts" in the US administration.

A meeting of the governing board of the International Energy Agency (IEA) is taking place tomorrow.

Prices of petrol and diesel globally have skyrocketed since the outbreak of the US-Israel war in Iran in February. The closure of the vital Strait of Hormuz, which typically transports around a fifth of the world's oil and gas, has pushed up the price of products made from oil.

An export ban from Russia, also a major supplier of diesel, has added to the pressure on prices.

Trump has argued that keeping any surplus barrels of diesel in the US would lower pump prices domestically, offering immediate relief to drivers, truckers, and businesses ahead of the midterm elections.

But David Fyfe, chief economist at Argus Media, said cutting off American supply would likely cause international prices to skyrocket.

Diesel prices have hit an all-time high in the UK, with the latest RAC figures showing average pump prices at 199.79p per litre, up from 142.38p

Diesel is harder to refine than gasoline and, because it is used by the haulage industry and in agriculture, it is very difficult to reduce demand.

The UK is heavily reliant on imports. Although the four refineries in the UK make more than enough petrol to meet demand, they do not make enough diesel for the country's needs.

There were 15.1 million diesel vehicles on UK roads at the end of June, according to the Department for Transport. That is a drop from 15.7 million a year before.

There were 9.8 million diesel cars, down year on year from 10.4 million.

Until early September, Hassan Nassar, 26, was saving around £430 every month into his NHS workplace pension.

But the trainee GP, who works in the West Midlands, says he was "really cash strapped" and decided to stop putting money aside for around "six to 12 months".

He needs the money to help take care of a sick family member, save for his first home and cover rent and student loan repayments.

But he's aware there is a cost to opting out, estimating he could lose between "£5,000 and £10,000" in future retirement income due to the decades of compound interest he will miss out on by not saving now.

"People will say, you're silly, look at what you'll be missing out in the future," he tells the BBC. "But I need to look at what I'd be losing now if I didn't opt out."

All employees will be automatically enrolled , external in a workplace pension if they are aged 22 or above and earn over £10,000, although there are exceptions.

A percentage is taken directly from the worker's pay - usually around 5% - with tax relief added on top, and the employer must also pay a minimum contribution on top.

But a growing number of Gen Z and millennials are opting out of these schemes due to cost-of-living pressures and the government has warned they could be on track for lower private pension incomes than people retiring today.

That is a problem, because while most people in the UK will eventually get a state pension , it only provides a minimum level of retirement income and many will rely on a private pension to supplement it.

Hassan says he was paying 10.7% of his gross earnings each month into his workplace pension, while the NHS contributed a substantial amount on top.

But unlike some employers, the NHS doesn't allow staff to reduce their contributions when times are hard.

Overall, however, he is confident he will have enough to retire on at the end of his "30-40" year career and is determined to opt back in to his pension as soon as he can.

According to the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP), around 22.6 million people, or 90% of those who are eligible for "automatic enrolment" pensions, are paying into one, while about 2.5 million are not.

However, Pensions Minister Torsten Bell told the BBC that "a rising number of young workers aren't saving, and overall there is a danger tomorrow's retirees are on track for lower private pension incomes than today's".

In the three months to December last year, 11.5% of eligible 22 to 29-year-olds who recently started a job opted out of their pensions. That's up from 6.6% in the same period of 2020.

For 30 to 39-year-olds it's gone from 7.4% to 12.7%.

Evie, 22, from Cornwall, says she opted out of entering the workplace pension at the London events company she works for.

A recent drama school graduate, she says she would have struggled to cover her outgoings, including food, travel and the £800 she pays in rent.

Evie is conscious about missing out on saving for retirement, but there are other things she needs money for that make it impractical right now.

"How can I save for a house, how can I save for a car and afford my outgoings? I don't want to just work day in, day out to live, I want to work to have a life."

April Leeson, from The Private Office, a chartered financial advice firm, says she would always advise people to not stop paying into their pensions if they can help it, even if that means reducing their contributions, which many employers allow you to do.

This is partly because of the free employer contributions they will miss out on but also the lost compound interest.

"The current minimum pension age is 57, so any money you save in your 20s will have at least 30 years to compound and grow.

"£100 saved now, compounded at 4% a year over 30 years, is going to be worth a lot more than £100 saved in 15 to 20 years' time."

She also urges younger people to think ahead. "You really need to think of your future self and what that person will need to retire comfortably."

Kharlee, 47, a teacher from South East London, can certainly relate to this. She stopped her contributions to a workplace pension twice over the last five years for financial reasons.

And she thinks she missed out on saving about £5,000 into her pension pot.

She's in a better place financially now, but recently became self-employed and is no longer part of a private pension scheme, something she hopes to change.

"I would like to feel my pension is secure, and I don't feel like that. I worry I'm not going to be able to live comfortably at the age of retirement."

Are you able to save money every month? Share your tips with us on how you do it.

Warning: This story contains distressing details

A businessman was beaten with hammers by masked men who broke into his home and threatened to kill his heavily pregnant wife unless he transferred hundreds of thousands of pounds of cryptocurrency.

Speaking to the BBC, the couple, who want to remain anonymous, described the attack as "horrific" and said they feared for their unborn baby's life.

The attackers left in a car driven by a getaway driver after the man transferred his crypto savings.

Crimestoppers are offering a £10,000 reward for information in the attack, which was captured on home security footage and is being investigated by the police.

Experts say it is one of a growing type of violent theft known as a "wrench attack" targeting cryptocurrency investors.

As crypto coins have risen in value, reports of these violent robberies linked to digital assets have emerged in the UK, France and the US.

Once funds are transferred, recovering them can be extremely difficult.

The man, who the BBC is calling James, said three intruders forced their way into their Solihull home before launching an assault which lasted 45 minutes.

"The door gets pushed open, I can see gloves coming in, balaclavas," he said.

James tried to fight the men off but they hit him in the face, head and ribs with hammers.

His wife, who was seven months pregnant, was held down on the sofa by one of the criminals.

"He's got a pillow over her face," James said. "He's literally suffocating her on the sofa. I can hear her screaming, 'I can't breathe'."

The couple still had no idea what the criminals wanted until one of the men demanded James unlock his phone and hand it over.

James said the attackers appeared to know he owned cryptocurrency, but had little understanding of how to access it.

Instead, they were taking instructions from someone else connected via a live video call.

"I can hear the guy on FaceTime saying: 'Show me everything on his phone. Show me what apps he's got'," he said.

When the caller identified a crypto wallet containing substantial funds, the threats escalated dramatically.

"He was basically saying: 'Look, if you don't send us this money now, we're going to stab your wife in the stomach and kill your baby. We're going to kill your wife'," James said.

His wife, who also did not want to be named, described the attack that happened in December last year as "horrific" and said she feared James had been killed when he was unresponsive on the floor.

The woman, in her early thirties, was expecting her third child at the time and said she feared she might lose the baby due to the stress of the attack. The baby survived and was born at full term.

The men left after James transferred his savings - hundreds of thousands of pounds of cryptocurrency - to the digital wallet of the man on the video call.

They also stole several luxury Rolex watches.

James said before they left, he heard the man on the video call tell his accomplices: "You can have 10 grand each but I am taking the rest."

Unlike money held in a conventional bank account, cryptocurrency is often controlled directly by the owner through digital wallets or physical storage devices.

For criminals, that combination of speed, anonymity and irreversibility can make crypto holders attractive targets.

Whilst the vast majority of cryptocurrency theft happens online through hacks and scams, crypto investigators at Chainalysis say "wrench attacks" have surged in recent years.

According to their research, $30m (£22.6m) had been stolen so far this year up to June in violent robberies, making 2026 likely to become the single-worst year for violent crypto attacks on record. Home invasions are also on the rise this year, it found.

The US, Brazil, and Thailand are hotspots but France has seen the largest number of attacks by far, as a result of a data breach at a tax office that has apparently allowed wealthy crypto holders to be located.

"The physical security assumptions that protect traditional wealth, such as bank vaults and armored cars, do not automatically apply in crypto. Often, holders keep their assets in comparatively low security setups, like self-custody wallets, that can be compromised without any institutional gatekeeper standing in the way," said researchers in their report.

James said he became an amateur investor in crypto coins in 2020 and made enough money to quit his job in 2023 to trade full time.

Now he has lost everything and is looking to get back to his traditional job.

Police have yet to identify the attackers.

Crimestoppers is offering a £10,000 reward for information leading to progress in the investigation.

Alan Edwards from the charity hopes people might have information about the three attackers, the driver who was parked outside without a face covering, or the man on the phone.

"These criminals are obviously serious and part of some kind of organised crime gang," he said.

"People might be scared to give us information but we are independent of the police and keep people completely anonymous."

The three attackers are all thought to be in their late teens or early 20s and one of them was a black male with a scar under his left eyebrow.

James said he has little hope of recovering the stolen funds, but instead wanted to see those responsible brought to justice.

He also wants his experience to serve as a warning.

"They threatened my wife and my baby," he said. "People need to understand these risks are real."

The price of vapes is set to rise as a new tax comes into effect, with the aim of making vaping less attractive to children and young people.

The Vaping Product Duty will be imposed at a rate of £2.20 per 10ml of e-liquid. However, many customers will not see a jump in prices immediately, as sellers have six months to sell old stock at the pre-duty price.

The government wants to reduce the appeal of vapes by making them more expensive, as more evidence of its adverse effect on health comes out, particularly on children and young people.

The vaping industry has lobbied against the new tax, saying that affordable vapes help people to quit smoking.

The duty will apply to all vaping products regardless of whether they contain nicotine.

Tobacco rates were also raised on Thursday, by £2.20 per 100 cigarettes or 50g of tobacco. HMRC said this maintains the financial incentive for smokers to switch to vaping.

The BBC spoke to vapers in Reading who had mixed views on whether the new tax would encourage people to quit.

Mackenzie Bird, 19, has been a regular vaper for three years. She said she was "fine" with the duty and it wouldn't stop her from vaping.

"I don't know how many people it'll actually deter," she said.

However, Cara Lewis-Rimes and Dylan Killner said they might reconsider the habit in light of higher prices.

Cara said she thinks the changes will force vapers to cut down because of the cost of living.

Dylan said he might be inclined to quit altogether.

"I don't think it's doing me any favours... the health factor around it as well is not great."

HMRC is also launching a stamp for vaping products which are traceable throughout the supply chain.

All vapes sold in the UK must carry this stamp from April.

The new tax is also an effort to combat illicit trade, which is a growing problem on UK high streets . Last month, the prime minister announced new powers for councils that will address the decline of the high street, including the amount of vape shops.

Changes to planning law in England mean every new shop selling e-cigarettes, or vapes, would need to apply to their local council for permission to open.

Health Minister Karin Smyth said: "These measures are an important step in our ambition to tackle youth vaping by reducing the affordability of vaping products, which goes hand-in-hand with the work we are already doing to tackle the appeal and availability of vapes on our high streets."

James Murray, the Financial Secretary to the Treasury, said the government was "backing all those retailers who play by the rules".

But Jordan Apap, a sales assistant in Berkshire Vapers, said the new tax would "put a lot of strain on legitimate vape shops" that provide more specialist advice and services than convenience stores and phone shops that sell vapes.

"There is a real and genuine risk that we will cease to exist within a year or two," he said.

Vaping rates for schoolchildren appear to drop - is it falling out of favour?

Police raid barbers and vape shops suspected of being fronts for crime gangs

John Dunne, the director general of the UK Vaping Industry Association, said: "This is nothing short of a tax on public health."

He said vapes had helped "millions of adults cut down on or stop smoking".

"Protecting young people is essential. But that means stronger enforcement against illegal and rogue traders, not making legal vaping more expensive for adults trying to stay away from cigarettes."

Experts say vaping is much safer than smoking, but it is not risk free and the long-term effects are less clear.

A recent review of vaping studies found that it had an association with problems in children and young people including wheezing and coughing, poor oral and dental health, poor sleep, mental health problems and eye symptoms.

The NHS has said that children and non-smokers should never vape.

Additional reporting by Neranjana Elapatha
