Bacon has long been a favourite of carnivores, but there is growing consumer concern about the health risks posed by nitrites, chemicals used to cure meats.

While many experts argue there is no evidence processed meat made without nitrites is safer, retailers have responded to consumer concerns by offering “nitrite-free” products to meet demand.

Denhay, the Devon hand- dry-cured bacon specialist, has launched two new back bacon lines in 570 Tesco stores from 21 September – Made Without Nitrites Smoked Back Bacon and Made Without Nitrites Unsmoked Back Bacon (both 200g), both priced at £4.

Waitrose has doubled its Made Without Nitrites range in the past year, with sales up more than 34%. Sales of its British roast and honey roast hams have risen more than 70% since launching in May, and its unsmoked back bacon is up 22%.

Data from Worldpanel by Numerator shows nitrite-free bacon growing steadily while conventional bacon declines, and its share of the fresh bacon category has risen steadily from a small base. In the 52 weeks to 6 September 2026, nitrite-free spend reached £34.8m (up 11.4% year on year) and volumes were up to 2.2m kg (up 8.0%), while spend and volume for conventional bacon was 9.2% and 4.9%, respectively.

Emer Lowry, a nutritionist at Waitrose, said: “As our customers pay closer attention to on-pack ingredient lists, providing options without added nitrites gives shoppers more choice without compromising on flavour and taste.”

Marlene Godwin, the managing director of Denhay, said the move was prompted by retailers and shoppers rather than the producer. “We definitely don’t want to be telling people what to eat. This is about giving bacon lovers choice, not replacement. Retailers were saying customers want this, can you provide it?

She added: “I can’t speak for shoppers, but I think health consciousness is driving it, and consumers are more interested. One of the things people said to me was, why not convert everything? Our customers still love traditional cure, but we’re offering another choice.”

Sodium and potassium nitrates and nitrites are chemicals that are often used to preserve or “cure” meat.

Nitrates, which contain one nitrogen and three oxygens atoms, can be converted by bacteria into nitrites, which contain one nitrogen and two oxygen atoms.

Nitrites help to prevent the growth of microbes, including harmful bacteria, and can enhance the flavour and pink colour of meat products.

People do not consume these chemicals only through eating meat – nitrates are also provided by vegetables, in particular leafy greens.

The Food Standards Agency (FSA) says the key difference is that when nitrates or nitrites are consumed as part of protein-rich foods such as meat, they are converted into chemicals known as nitrosamines, which are thought to be harmful to health.

“Vegetables provide nitrates alongside beneficial nutrients such as vitamin C, polyphenols and fibre. These nutrients help to reduce the formation of harmful nitrosamines,” the FSA adds

The World Health Organization’s cancer agency classes processed meat as a group 1 carcinogen , the same category as tobacco, though the known link between processed meat and cancer cannot be directly attributed to nitrites.

Research suggests eating about 50g of processed meat a day , roughly two rashers of bacon, is linked to a 16% higher relative risk of colorectal cancer.

The FSA says no single component of processed meat has been identified as the cause , and there is no definitive evidence that nitrites directly cause cancer.

The FSA also says there is no evidence that processed meats made without nitrate or nitrite additives are safer . It adds that removing them can create food safety challenges, because they help prevent the growth of dangerous bacteria and must be replaced by other methods of preservation.

Gabriela Peacock, a nutritionist and founder of GP Nutrition , said: “People are much more interested in what is actually in their food now. They are turning packets over, reading ingredient lists and looking for products that feel a little less processed. If someone enjoys bacon or ham but sees an option made without added nitrates, it can feel like a very easy, positive swap, without having to change the way they eat completely.”

Peacock said nitrite-free products are often more expensive. “That may be because they are made by smaller producers, use different curing methods or have a shorter shelf life. They may also use higher-welfare meat or more expensive ingredients. Sometimes, of course, you are paying for the premium positioning and packaging too,” she said.

She added: “The most expensive option is not automatically the healthiest, just as ‘nitrate-free’ does not give a product a magic health halo. Nitrates and nitrites help to preserve meat and control harmful bacteria, and the Food Standards Agency says there is currently no evidence that processed meat made without them is safer.”

15-year-old wants his registration to be cancelled

He was to be in squad to face Brighton on Wednesday

Manchester United have been left confused and shocked by the news that the talented 15-year-old player JJ Gabriel has asked to leave the club, a day before he was to be included in the first-team squad to face Brighton.

Gabriel could have become United’s youngest player in the Carabao Cup third-round tie at Old Trafford on Wednesday. But the Guardian understands he has asked for his registration to be cancelled.

United are unsure what has prompted this decision and believe they have done everything they can to show Gabriel and his family there is a pathway to the first team. Those efforts have included meetings with Ruben Amorim, when the Portuguese was head coach, and Sir Alex Ferguson.

United believe the situation, first reported by the Telegraph , is rectifiable given the time remaining on Gabriel’s contract. Club officials say the player has a deal to the end of the season and cannot be deregistered despite his request. The north London-born Gabriel cannot sign a professional contract until he turns 17 in October next year, but can sign a scholarship agreement when he turns 16.

Gabriel, who has been with United since the age of 11, has emerged as one of the most exciting prospects at Carrington in years, scoring a hatful of goals for the youth teams, most recently a hat-trick on his Uefa Youth League debut against Sabah last week. He regularly plays for older age groups at United, scoring 26 goals in 29 games last season, and has made two appearances for England Under-17s. Gabriel is also the most recent, and youngest, winner of United’s prestigious Jimmy Murphy young player of the year award. He has regularly trained with the first team.

Speaking after that 5-0 win against Sabah, Adam Lawrence, United’s lead under-21 coach, said: “JJ is surrounded by people that really, really believe in him from the top of the club right the way through. He’s been at the club for so long. He’s got real good relationships with the players, with the staff, so I think over the course of time obviously that helps as well.

“At the moment, just in terms of his game, his games programme, his training programme, it’s about making sure that he’s getting the right exposure across different levels. We’re obviously not perfect but it’s definitely something we put a lot of thought into.”

Barcelona and Manchester City have been linked previously with Gabriel, after reports emerged last year suggesting the player’s family would be planning to move him.

Across four days Manchester United have lost the 199th derby against Manchester City, were told by JJ Gabriel that he wants to leave , and now they have been knocked out of the Carabao Cup by Brighton.

Capitulating after being 2-0 up may be the pick of these dizzying blows, as the prolonged boos at the final whistle suggested, and doing so ends a proud 50-year record: the last time the same lead at Old Trafford ended in defeat was Tottenham’s 3-2 win in September 1976.

When Marcus Rashford skated in with the chance to take the tie to 3-3 late on, there was no surprise he hit Jason Steele rather than the net.

Towards the end, Matheus Cunha was thrown on to join Bruno Fernandes, also a late substitute, illustrating how desperate Michael Carrick was. Yet Charalampos Kostoulas went close to scoring a second for Brighton, as United could not find a route to cancelling out Maxim De Cuyper’s 69th-minute strike that proved the winner.

After taking only four points from 12 in the league, serious questions will now be asked about where Carrick’s team are heading; they have to beat Fulham on Sunday to start correcting a dismal start to the season . The manager already looks haunted and he talked afterwards of not caring about being under pressure.

Carrick said the injustice suffered against City on Sunday would give his side an edge and Shea Lacey provided one when decorating a full debut with the sweetest of goals. The 19-year-old shimmied in Brighton’s area, beating Jaouen Hadjam before firing beyond a helpless Jason Steele. As impressive here was Benjamin Sesko’s hold-up work in the buildup as this allowed red shirts to flood forward, Youri Tielemans feeding Lacey.

This was eight minutes in and less than 120 seconds later Mason Mount doubled United’s advantage. Rashford’s pace and drive took him clear along the left, again inside the area. A trailing Steele boot saved the No 9’s effort but the ball bounced into Mount’s path and he drove home, via the turf, for a first goal since a win at Wolves last December .

Lacey’s strike drew a Carrick grin and delight from Mount, and you wondered how Gabriel – earmarked for the squad in this game, with the chance to become United’s youngest player – felt.

Brighton had lost only one of their previous five visits here and a flying start to the league campaign has Fabian Hürzeler’s team in fifth. Yet the 5-0 hammering of Coventry on Sunday already seemed distant as United continued to dominate.

Olivier Boscagli hit a corner straight out, summing up the visitors’ start, before Matt O’Riley forced Ayden Heaven into an error that led to another. This presaged a Seagulls renaissance that featured a lightning Malick Yalcouyé break but, clear in on the debutant Karl Darlow’s goal, the Ivorian spooned wide. The No 35 lacked the sharpness evident in a Rashford nutmeg of Chema Andrés which embarrassed the Brighton man and when Pascal Gross blasted over this was one more chance spurned by Hürzeler’s men.

But then came a goal – and real hope – for Brighton. Hadjam’s long left-right diagonal cut United’s rearguard clean out, and the slumbering Heaven allowed Kostoulas to scamper free, the striker beating Darlow through his legs.

Carrick, having beaten only Ipswich in the league and Sabah in Europe so far this season, needed a win, and as United (not under him) exited at the earliest opportunity in both domestic cups last season, progressing to at least a second tie in one of them would be welcome.

A wild Tielemans long-range shot that ballooned over failed to restore United’s two-goal lead but at least the home team were tapping the ball about, operating in Brighton territory, moving the visitors around.

A Sesko burst from halfway had the onrushing Steele hacking away just in time. United were in control. But the question was: could they maintain this and register the type of mature, accomplished display that would show an evolution in Carrick’s team? Sesko, in yards of space, dawdling and being dispossessed when a simple ball would have fed Lacey, suggested not.

A loose Rashford pass aimed for Sesko hinted at the same. More promising was a pass for Noussair Mazraoui as he drove into the area along the left channel, as was the subsequent corner that created an opening Tielemans narrowly missed.

But then calamity. Diogo Dalot’s hoofed clearance failed to find Sesko as Luka Vuskovic headed to Gross; Brighton’s captain made room and netted with ease. Even worse followed. Brighton raided along the right, Kostoulas’s cross pinged off Mazraoui’s backside, and there was De Cuyper to finish.

On 72 minutes Carrick played his ace, introducing Fernandes for Mount, then followed up with Cunha. But United remained toothless.

‘I take responsibility … it doesn’t feel good at the moment’

United beaten 3-2 by Brighton after taking two-goal lead

Michael Carrick admitted Manchester United’s Carabao Cup capitulation against Brighton that was greeted by boos at Old Trafford was unacceptable and that answers had to be found at Fulham on Sunday.

United were knocked out 3-2 by Fabian Hürzeler’s visitors after leading 2-0 after 10 minutes through Shea Lacey and Mason Mount. Goals from Charalampos Kostoulas in first‑half added time, Pascal Gross on 65 minutes and Maxim De Cuyper four minutes later eliminated United.

It was the first time United had lost after leading 2-0 at Old Trafford for 50 years and the first time since 1984 they had been defeated there after being ahead at half-time.

Carrick’s side have beaten only Ipswich in the league and Sabah in the Champions League . “Under pressure? That doesn’t bother me one bit,” he said.

“I understand what goes on and how the world works. What bothers me is winning games and I believe we will do, but we have to do it pretty quickly. We can’t accept that [the manner of the defeat] as a group. I take responsibility for it. The performance towards the end of the second half, that’s on me. We have a big game on Sunday that we have to prepare for. We’re out of this competition and we have to go back to winning football matches. It doesn’t feel good at the moment.”

Carrick said of the boos at the end: “I totally understand the feelings of the supporters.”

The manager was asked about JJ Gabriel, the 15-year-old academy player who has informed United he wants to leave . “We have to be a little bit careful on that one. He’s a 15-year-old boy. Recruitment is under scrutiny after £155m was spent on three midfielders while other positions were neglected

T here was a mix of boos and apathy as Manchester United slumped out of the Carabao Cup on Wednesday in their latest depressing act in domestic cup competitions. A solemn Michael Carrick and his players were the target for the jeers. The director of football, Jason Wilcox, looked unamused on his way out of the directors’ box but he and the hierarchy need to accept responsibility for their actions.

This is the natural course of football, where supporters know what is good or bad and give a rapid opinion to those whose wages they deem they pay. Carrick and his charges are the face of the club, the ones put up to speak with journalists and sent to promote the wares of sponsors.

The head coach is often viewed as accountable for everything, from tactics to transfers, but the picture is more complex.

Carrick returned to United in January, but others have overseen the long-term strategy, within which the head coach sits. Pressure comes with his job, though, and a loss at Fulham on Sunday would significantly increase it.

United’s fanbase is fully aware of those running the club, with regular protests against the Glazer family and Sir Jim Ratcliffe. They realise not everything happening over 90 minutes is the fault of the head coach and those wearing the shirt. The boos are for the one-off performance, the apathy for the bigger picture. It is tough for United supporters to see their club, back in the Champions League, outspent in the summer by promoted sides but this is the reality after years of financial mismanagement. It means the funds available have to be spent wisely.

United being two goals ahead against Brighton after 10 minutes and deservedly losing a game they were barely involved in for the remaining 80 is a strong indication things are not right within the team but Carrick knows this. Brighton were much changed but possess an exciting array of talent acquired from all over the world thanks to clever scouting and recruitment. They signed players from clubs in seven countries this summer, while United made four acquisitions from fellow Premier League clubs. Calculated risks and dynamism are part of the job but rarely seen at Old Trafford. It is somewhat ironic considering the most successful acquisition last summer was Senne Lammens from Royal Antwerp, in terms of price and consistency.

Carrick and Wilcox cannot truly be analysed until the most expensive of the three summer buys, Carlos Baleba, is available because his attributes should solve the lack of mobility. Targeting central midfielders was logical after the exit of Casemiro and inadequacy of Manuel Ugarte, but it was not the only area requiring attention. The overall deficiency of the squad was acknowledged internally but the lack of variety in strengthening felt naive and is proving to be so.

Buying players from other Premier League clubs is rarely cost-effective but there is a logic to limiting the adaptation time. Given the left-back shortage and Joshua Zirkzee’s inadequacies, sourcing a cheaper midfield option than the £50m Andrey Santos could have been advantageous for the wider health of the team. Someone needs to alleviate the pressure on Carrick by explaining why it was deemed best to spend £155m on three players in the same position. The outside world is left to pontificate, while Carrick creates a plan B when Luke Shaw, as many anticipated, has time out injured.

Wilcox has carried out internal media duties. On 30 October 2025, after three consecutive wins, he discussed the long-term plan, which was derailed by sacking Ruben Amorim just over two months later. Matters were going well when Wilcox opened up to United’s editorial staff but, apart from statements on sackings, he shows no appetite to speak amid downturns.

In Europe, sporting directors talking to the press is normal but the Premier League is yet to catch on, and the silence mounts at United with the team 13th.

Wilcox arrived, originally as technical director, from Southampton in 2024 and helped oversee the retention of Erik ten Hag after an eighth-placed finish. Ten Hag was belatedly dismissed for a poor start to the next season. Amorim was hired from Sporting despite his tactics not matching up with the squad available and a lack of finance to provide the overhaul required. United ended 15th and endured a meek Europa League final defeat by Tottenham. When Amorim was dismissed for his shortcomings after 14 months, Wilcox was permitted another chance to rectify the situation.

Carrick is not absolved of criticism; this United team are underperforming and pummelling promoted Ipswich and the Azerbaijan side Sabah cannot mask the disappointing start.

The defence has struggled, conceding seven goals in four Premier League games, and against Brighton the pairing of Leny Yoro and Ayden Heaven was bordering on inept. The forward line has looked disjointed.

Wilcox was well respected when working as Manchester City’s head of academy, and those who dealt with him thought he was exceptional and suited to a role at that level. He is scrutinised and criticised for his work at United after moving up the chain. Many on the outside will be frustrated if JJ Gabriel departs but Wilcox would not be culpable, having worked hard to convince the player to stay, including via the teenager’s inner circle.

With power comes great responsibility at United but only Carrick is forced to embrace it. Ten Hag and Amorim have fallen for their failures, while others have been allowed to carry on. Carrick and Wilcox are equally invested in the success of the team but it seems only one will feel the consequences if things do not improve.

To paraphrase a former Manchester United manager, Michael Carrick knew that the storm would come. Everything went a little too perfectly for him in the second half of last season. There would be ill winds at some point. Which was what Carrick could feel before this visit to Fulham. What were his emotions afterwards?

Relief was surely the main thing. Because after the derby defeat by Manchester City last Sunday and the midweek Carabao Cup exit against Brighton – both at Old Trafford – Carrick was starring at an unwanted hat-trick. All this on the back of other wobbles since the opening weekend when United lost at Hull. It is all extremely angsty and edgy.

It was a darkly comic own goal by Lisandro Martínez that raised Fulham’s hopes of a first Premier League win under Álvaro Arbeloa; an episode in which the United goalkeeper, Senne Lammens, emerged with zero credit. Put it down as a colossal mess. United have almost always won in this corner of south‑west London in recent seasons. A crash against the team that started the day at the foot of the table was unthinkable.

Carrick and his side averted disaster when they caught a huge break with time almost up. There was little on for Matheus Cunha on the edge of the area, to the left of centre, and so he took on the shot for the near corner. The Fulham goalkeeper, Bernd Leno, looked to have it covered. Cue an almighty deflection off David Affengruber that sent the ball spinning into the opposite corner. United escaped.

It was true that Fulham invited pressure after the own goal. They sank back and came to lack an out‑ball. But it did not look as though United would find the required moment. Carrick’s players were too slow. Their moves were predictable. They could not get in behind in the second half, their only efforts coming from outside the area. Thankfully for Carrick, Cunha got one to work.

There was plenty to like about Fulham, who remain a work in progress under Arbeloa. He appears to have concluded that he needs greater security in central midfield – hence Sander Berge an d Shea Charles, with Alex Iwobi moved out to the left wing. There were round pegs in round holes for Fulham, which was not completely the case for United, albeit they were able to welcome back Luke Shaw on the left side of their defence.

With no Benjamin Sesko because of a recurrence of his shin issue, Carrick was without his only pure No 9. His solution, once again, was to use Cunha as a false 9 and ask Bruno Fernandes to play close to him. It was a box midfield, with Youri Tielemans and Kobbie Mainoo further back.

Arbeloa got his wingers, Oscar Bobb and Iwobi, to come inside to good effect. The battle for control of the middle of the pitch pulsed, with Josh King a major part of it.

The No 10 threatened during a first half in which Fulham were the more urgent and creative team. King worked Lammens in the 32nd minute after buying a yard of space from Shaw and it was not the only time that United felt their hearts skip.

Fulham had to be annoyed that they did not score before the interval. Twice, Gonzalo García fluffed his finish when well placed; on the second occasion, Berge extended Lammens on the second phase of the move. There was also the moment when Bobb spun into a seam of space only to drag wide. King wanted a free‑kick on the edge of the area in the 45th minute after running into Harry Maguire but he was looking for the contact and was booked correctly for diving.

United hit the woodwork twice in the first half and had other flickers. They got into some good positions only to lack composure. Cunha did well to wriggle clear of Affengruber on the right and pull back for Fernandes, who flicked against the far post. Cunha also saw his first deflected shot of the day loop high and drop down against the outside of the upright. Martínez forced Leno into a decent save early on. Marcus Rashford lifted a good chance high.

United lost their way after the restart. They lacked energy and could get nothing going. It was as if they hit a wall, and then came the gut punch of the own goal. It started when Cunha failed to hold up the ball in a deep midfield position. He was outmuscled by Calvin Bassey, who simply wanted it more. The Fulham captain pushed on to the edge of the area and when he unloaded, United’s problems were about to deepen.

Lammens’s parry was unconvincing and Martínez was ponderous. He could not set his feet properly and merely jabbed the ball towards his own goal – whereupon Lammens, perhaps wondering whether it was a back pass, tried to clear with his feet and got it all wrong.

United could feel the red panic lights flashing. They fought to stabilise and the plus point for Carrick was that his players kept going. Bryan Mbeumo and Cunha forced Leno into fine saves with curlers from distance. The key point was that they were from distance. It is a symbol of the connection between the fanbase and club, but there is a growing fear executives would prefer stadiums full of one-off tourists

T he document known as “the oldest football season ticket in the world” promises its bearer access to every Burnley home game of the 1884-85 season. It is a ticket that predates the Football League by four years, with all the fixtures played against east Lancashire neighbours. All the same, the legend on the ticket carries a stern warning: “This card is not transferable. Any member violating this rule will be at once expelled from the club.”

For Burnley 1884 read Manchester United 2026. While the oldest remaining season ticket is preserved safely at Turf Moor, at Old Trafford 685 season tickets were voided this summer after a club investigation found evidence of their having been resold on the secondary market. United said such practices “undermine fair access to tickets for genuine supporters and have no place at Manchester United”. United fan groups again protested against the actions of the club’s ownership, claiming: “The way you treat us is a disgrace.”

Nearly 150 years after fans started paying up front to watch their team, the season ticket remains a key component in the success of English football. It is also an enduring source of conflict between supporters and clubs, with tensions seemingly reaching new heights.

Arsenal, like United, have continued to act against the perceived misuse of tickets, suspending nearly 74,000 club accounts since they began a crackdown in 2024. This summer Chelsea became the latest club to insist on minimum levels of attendance to retain your ticket for the following season. Bournemouth moved 600 season-ticket holders to accommodate new hospitality seats and 14 out of the 20 top-flight sides raised their season-ticket prices.

Season-ticket holders have long felt undervalued. But there is a growing sense, especially among fans of the biggest clubs, that they are falling ever further down the pecking order as economic imperatives change. It is a feeling that intensified after a World Cup that seemed precision-tooled to extract as much money as possible from the most devoted fans. One Liverpool supporter crystallised common fears when he appeared on The Overlap at the start of the season arguing that a big club would soon try to get rid of season tickets altogether. The clip went viral.

The Football Supporters’ Association argues that clubs’ present behaviour shows an antagonism towards season-ticket holders. “There’s a sense from supporter groups at the most successful teams that their club executives and owners don’t fully appreciate season ticket holders and would rather have stadiums full of one-off visitors,” an FSA spokesperson said.

“Those who only measure things by the bottom line see season-ticket holders as a group whose matchday spend is lower than the once-a-year fan who will fill their bag at the club shop and pay a bigger premium for their ticket. It’s a shortsighted vision.”

The claim that clubs want to swap longstanding supporters for one-off tourists is at the heart of many fans’ fears over season tickets and, to a certain extent, it bears out. Dominik Schreyer, a professor of sports economics at the WHU Otto Beisheim School of Management in Düsseldorf, says season tickets “come at a cost” for clubs.

“In the Premier League , demand is way higher than seat supply,” Schreyer says. “But season-ticket holders get discounted seats, right? They are also more likely to be no-shows. When they do come they spend less on food, less on merchandise and they come later to the stadium. They also don’t churn, because these tickets are so scarce that nobody in their right mind would give them away. Every year the average age grows by one because there is no one new getting tickets. So for the clubs, there are a lot of economic problems from their season-ticket holders.”

That, however, is only one side of the ledger. “What we should not forget is that, in the end, season‑ticket holders are part of a product that, in the case of the Premier League, is marketed to a global audience,” Schreyer says.

“They are creating an atmosphere. Season-ticket holders are also used to all the rules and the rituals and the songs, the moments that make this experience very special. So tourists want to come because they want to experience it. If you were to get rid of all the season-ticket holders, you would have all the operational and coordination costs of doing it and the product would not be the same any more.”

There are other reasons why season tickets work for clubs, not least because they generate a largely predictable amount of revenue that turns up at the same time each year (at the very end of the season where it can be usefully deployed to help with transfer spending limits).

For most clubs, it would not be feasible to replace season‑ticket holders with one-off fans even if they wanted to. But with the average number of season tickets at any given Premier League fixture running at 75% of all tickets, is there a case that this number should not be set in stone? Could access to matches be broadened without killing off a part of what made them great?

“In theory, you could give all the seats to season-ticket holders and still have a lot of tickets for new fans if you manage it effectively,” Schreyer says. “You just need to change the mechanism in order to get the ticket that is unused on to the secondary market.”…

Billy Meredith helped win City their first major honours more than a hundred years ago, was banned by the FA – then went and repeated the trick on the red side of Manchester

W hen the Manchester City decision finally dropped, the Guardian’s verdict was damning. “FOOTBALL SENSATION – MANCHESTER CITY’S GRAVE OFFENCES – HEAVY PUNISHMENTS”, the headline read. “It is now proved that the club had for years systematically broken the rules of the Football Association by very unscrupulous means.”

But these words weren’t written last Friday . Instead they were penned more than 120 years ago, at the culmination of English football’s first big illicit payments scandal.

Back then City were a club rapidly on the up, with money and attitude to burn – which might sound familiar. Yet having won the FA Cup in 1904, everything began to unravel.

It started on the final day of the 1905 season, when City were on the verge of winning the title only to lose against Aston Villa in a match that involved punches and literal mud-slinging . Far more seriously, City’s star player, Billy Meredith, was also heard offering a £10 bribe to the Villa captain, Alec Leake, to throw the game.

Some say it was not serious. To this day no one knows the mysterious spectator who reported it. But it created a butterfly effect that led to Meredith being suspended for a season, and ramifications that lasted for decades.

Soon after, when Meredith was seen still hanging around City despite his ban, the FA launched a fresh investigation into the club’s finances. It found that not only was City’s gate money being funnelled into the private accounts of club directors, it was being used to give off-the-books payments to players.

Meredith, for instance, was on £6 a week when the maximum wage was £4. And he was far from the only one being given a little extra on the side. It led to the FA banning 17 players from playing for City again, while two of the club’s directors were banned for life.

History doesn’t repeat itself, but it does rhyme. So is what happened to City all those years ago relevant to modern times? Yes, absolutely.

First off, the 1906 case proves that strong punishments work. While City were hardly the only club to be making similar illicit payments, the FA’s sanctions led to the club slipping down the table, being relegated three years later, and not winning the title until 1937.

That City team also offered an early example of one of football’s immutable laws of gravity. The faster a club rises, the more its foundations may be shaky or unsustainable, and the more it is likely to plummet back to earth.

The other interesting thing in all this? While City had the book thrown at them , Meredith enjoyed a redemption arc that continues to this day.

It helped that some felt he had been unfairly targeted for trying to set up a players’ union and campaigning for the abolition of the maximum wage. The wiry winger could certainly play too, which certainly didn’t hurt either.

Indeed no less a judge than David Lacey, the Guardian’s legendary football correspondent, described Meredith as ranking “with that of Stanley Matthews in the history of the British game”.

And when Manchester United fans voted Eric Cantona as their greatest ever player in 2001, Lacey suggested that a couple of decades earlier they would have gone for George Best, and before that Meredith himself.

The fact that Meredith, who turned out for City from 1894 to 1905 and again from 1921 to 1924, is also in United’s hall of fame marks him out as a unique and substantial force.

Intriguingly, those switches across Manchester don’t appear to have attracted much condemnation. Indeed, when Meredith played in the Manchester derby in 1910, the Guardian’s man on the ground was left unimpressed by the lack of fire and venom.

“Both sides tried hard, no doubt; there was no shirking to speak of,” he wrote. “But the game differed in no way that one could see from a hundred other games in which local rivalry has had no place whatsoever. The teams might have represented Penzance and Berwick-on-Tweed respectively for all the evidence the play gave to the contrary.”

In echoes of more modern times, the Guardian’s man also questioned whether modern players cared enough about the shirt on their backs.

“Is it reasonable to expect local or even club fervour in professional football as it exists today?” he wrote after United had won 2-1. “Can local patriotism thrive under a red jersey this year, a blue one the next, and perhaps a white one after that? It does not seem likely.”

Incredibly, Meredith kept playing until he was 49, helped, as the Guardian noted in his obituary, by being a details man whose “mind persistently dwelt on the problems of the game”.

Meredith, who was affectionately known as “old skin” and played with a toothpick in his mouth to help him concentrate, eventually called it a day four months before his 50th birthday when he took over a pub.

Not that it was a quiet retirement. During the Manchester blitz , for instance, a bomb exploded at the back of the pub and a shower of Welsh international caps scattered across the local neighbourhood. It took some time to collect them all given he played 51 times for his country.

Meredith was certainly a smart cookie too. When he was asked about the secret of City’s success, he openly admitted it was because the “club put aside the rule that no player should receive more than £4 a week”.

“Clubs are not punished for breaking the law – they are punished for being found out,” he also admitted. Which applies as much to 2026 as it did all more than a century ago.

Manchester City have kicked off the campaign with five victories in a row but the title race is a marathon not a sprint

T he first international window gives us time to take stock and make sense of what has happened in the early weeks of the Premier League season. Manchester City are the only team to have won all five of their matches. They have started life after Pep Guardiola in the best way possible on the pitch, opening a three-point gap over champions Arsenal, but how important is a fast start?

Of course, we do not yet know the punishment they may face for breaking the Premier League’s financial fair play rules so, for the purposes of this article, we will put that matter to the side.

Enzo Maresca’s side became the 15th different team to win their opening five games of a Premier League season, and it’s the fourth occasion City have managed it. They have only won the title in one of the three previous seasons, though. They won the league in 2023-24, but failed to capitalise on their five early wins in 2015-16 and 2016-17.

That follows a wider trend across the league. Only four of the 14 teams that have won their first five matches of the season have gone on to win the title (29%): Manchester City in 2023-24, Liverpool in 2019-20, and Chelsea in 2009-10 and 2005-06.

Perhaps most importantly, all four teams went on to add to their winning streak to start those seasons. Chelsea in 2009-10 and Manchester City in 2023-24 extended their run by another game (six wins); Liverpool started with eight wins in 2019-20; and Chelsea (nine wins in 2005-06) went on the longest winning run to start a Premier League season.

Tottenham hold the record for the most consecutive wins to start a top-flight league season. They won their first 11 games in 1960-61 and, unsurprisingly, won the title that campaign. But a winning start does not guarantee success, as Manchester United found in 1985-86. Despite winning their first 10 games that season (and remaining unbeaten in their first 15) under Ron Atkinson, they collapsed and ended the season in fourth place.

It must be said, City have benefited from having an easy run of fixtures. According to the Opta Power Rankings , City had the second-easiest start this season, with their opponents having an average rating of 91.2. Only Liverpool (91.1) were handed a simpler start to the season by the Premier League fixture computer.

Another statistic that will give City fans reason for pause is that none of the previous seven clubs to start a Premier League season with exactly five wins have gone on to win the title in that campaign.

The most recent of those was Liverpool last season. The reigning champions won games against Bournemouth, Newcastle, Arsenal , Burnley and Everton to open the 2025-26 campaign before losing four in a row. The fact Liverpool won four of their first five games with goals scored after the 83rd minute pointed to their run being unsustainable, and so it proved.

Question marks about City’s defensive qualities this season suggest this may be another unsustainable winning run. Their credentials will be tested when the Premier League returns and they visit Anfield to face Liverpool, who are still unbeaten under new boss Andoni Iraola.

The lowest position a team has finished after winning their first five games of a season is sixth (Newcastle United in 1994-95), although that did come in a 42-game campaign. Looking back at all English top-flight history, City’s current streak is the 40th different occasion of a team winning their first five games in a season. Just 14 of the previous 39 have gone on to win the league title (36%).

The average points won by Premier League champions from the first five games across the previous 34 Premier League campaigns is 11.3, which is above the total secured by Arsenal last season. They won 10 points from their first five games, dropping points by losing at Liverpool and drawing against Manchester City at home. Mikel Arteta’s side have started this season better this time around, winning 12 points from a possible 15, with their only blemish the shock 3-0 loss at Brighton.

The fewest points eventual Premier League champions have won from their first five games was in the inaugural season in 1992-93. Manchester United won only seven points from their first five matches (two wins, one draw and two defeats), but Alex Ferguson’s side recovered and finished 10 points clear of runners up Aston Villa after the 42-game season.

No team has won a Premier League title in a 38-game season after winning fewer than eight points from their first five matches. United have won the league four times after winning exactly eight points from their opening five games (in 1998-99, 2002-03, 2007-08 and 2008-09), with City replicating that feat in 2020-21. What we’re trying to say is, Hull City and Newcastle fans, it’s still possible.

The most astonishing turnaround by title winners has to be Sunderland ’s effort in 1912-13, though. They failed to win any of their first seven games, drawing two and losing the other five, but they went on to win the First Division title. With just two points for a win back then, it was easier for teams to recover from a run of poor results; a monumental comeback nevertheless.

Artwork created in Tahrir Square for Chinese president’s state visit to Egypt is painted over amid allegations it revived Afrocentric claims about Pharaohs’ origins

On the eve of Chinese president Xi Jinping’s state visit to Cairo last month, the city authorities were busy removing a 66-metre-long mural from the esteemed guest’s line of sight.

Depicting the Pharaoh Tutankhamun and Queen Nefertiti, the painting was among 40 murals commissioned to beautify the city for Xi’s arrival and was painted by volunteer youth group Rasmet Basma, in Tahrir Square.

But it drew a furious reaction for depicting the two historical figures with dark skin – angering those Egyptians who saw it as reviving Afrocentric claims about the Pharaohs’ origins. The artwork vanished under fresh paint just hours before Xi landed.

Now, Ahmed Moussa, the 22-year-old founder of Rasmet Basma, has admitted it was asked by the Cairo governorate to paint over its work, which had been prepared in just five days in late August.

The team used the AI programme ChatGPT to generate the designs, which volunteers then painted on to the wall.

Moussa said Cairo’s deputy governor and the head of the district had visited the site throughout the process and were impressed by the murals – until controversy began to build on social media.

“We used a golden-bronze tone that cast a kind of shadow on the faces at night, so they appeared dark-skinned,” Moussa said.

“We acknowledge our mistake in not consulting specialists in archaeology and art.”

Afrocentrism is a political movement asserting that ancient Egyptian civilisation was black African in origin and population.

One user asked whether anyone involved had “even seen what Nefertiti actually looked like”, while others accused Afrocentric groups of appropriating the images to claim Egyptians endorsed their theories.

Zahi Hawass, Egypt’s former antiquities minister, said the volunteers should not have been allowed to paint a city site as significant as Tahrir Square without expert oversight, and that the public outrage was justified.

“Claims linking ancient Egyptian civilisation to sub-Saharan Africa are nonsense,” Hawass said.

“Temple carvings from the late period show Egyptian kings depicted alongside captives from parts of Africa, Libya, Syria and Palestine, with the king himself not shown as dark-skinned,” he said.

This is just the latest episode in a long-running debate over the complexion of ancient Egyptians. In 2023, a Netflix documentary provoked discussion after casting a dark-skinned actor as Cleopatra, and a similar dispute flared in June 2024 after a guide reportedly gave an Afrocentric perspective of Egyptian history in Cairo’s Egyptian Museum.

Monica Hanna, an Egyptologist at the American University in Cairo, labelled Afrocentric claims “pseudoscience”. She said Egyptian society had always been ethnically diverse, from Nubian communities in the south to Mediterranean populations in the north.

“Technology and streaming felt liberating for a person who has a deep and wide music collection and a bad back. ‘Half my day’s pay goes to filling up my car’

British motorists face more pressure at the pumps after the average price of diesel climbed to a record £2 a litre.

The price of a litre at UK forecourts has risen 40.5% since late February, when the US-Israel war on Iran began disrupting supplies of crude and refined oil products from the Gulf, leading to cost increases across the economy.

The RAC motoring group said on Friday that the average price had reached 200.01p a litre, meaning the cost of filling up an average family car is now £110, nearly £32 more than before the Iran war.

Simon Williams, the head of policy at the RAC, said: “This is a pump price threshold that no one wanted to cross.”

The RAC figures measure the average cost of fuel, but in reality many forecourts have been selling diesel above £2 a litre for some time.

Petrol prices are also continuing to rise, with a litre of unleaded costing 174.1p on average, a 31.5% increase since 28 February, taking the cost of a typical tank to £96, just over £23 more than before the US-Iran conflict.

Earlier on Friday the transport minister Keir Mather sought to avert panic at the pumps, insisting the UK was not facing a diesel shortage, after Donald Trump threatened to cut off US supplies of the fuel.

The Trump administration has told Germany and France to release their diesel stockpiles to help ease soaring global energy prices or face a US export ban.

On Thursday, the UK opened talks with European allies over releasing emergency supplies, and Dan Jørgensen, the EU commissioner for energy, said on Friday that Europe was discussing the diesel reserves issue with all members of the International Energy Agency (IEA), not only the US.

In a video conference with G7 leaders, chaired by the French president, Emmanuel Macron, attenders discussed a proposal from the French government that European nations release 50m barrels of diesel from reserve supplies, and for members of the IEA to release 50m barrels of crude oil, Reuters reported.

The UK relies on the US for about 30% of its diesel, with the vast majority coming from mainland Europe, and has reserve supplies for 42 days.

Motorists and small businesses have been struggling with the increasing cost of filling up .

Williams added: “This will be very challenging for households and companies that drive a lot of miles, from commuters, haulage and delivery firms, businesses with large fleets all the way through to sole traders.

“In a cruel twist, it’s diesel vehicles, which were once considered the most cost-effective option for lengthy journeys, that are now burning a hole in people’s pockets.”

Capital Economics estimated that a ban on US exports of diesel could raise UK diesel prices from £2 a litre to £3 a litre and push inflation up to 5%, from 3.1% in August.

The fresh high was recorded after record fuel prices across Europe in recent weeks, which have ignited calls for political leaders to take action to protect consumers against rising cost pressures.

Inflation in the cost of road fuels has outpaced the surge in global oil markets due to a sharp drop in output from refineries damaged by war in the Middle East and in Russia.

Before the Ukraine war, Russia provided between 10% and 15% of the world’s diesel supplies. Another 10% of global diesel supplies transited through the strait of Hormuz from Gulf nations before Iran responded to the US-Israeli attacks by disrupting the strait.

Trump has pushed his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, to cease Kyiv’s drone and missile attacks on Russian refineries so they can help to relieve the global fuel squeeze.

The Middle East war has also pushed up household energy bills. This week the quarterly price cap rose by 4%, meaning a typical household in Great Britain will pay £1,723 a year. The cap is forecast to increase by a further 16%, equivalent to adding £276 to the average annual dual-fuel bill, to take it to £1,999, according to the leading forecaster Cornwall Insight.

Reports of talks among European nations to potentially release diesel and oil reserves fuelled a 2.5% fall in the price of Brent crude to $99.78 a barrel.

“This highlights that the main stress in the energy market is no longer crude availability, with Middle East flows recovering,” said Ole Hansen, the head of commodity strategy at Saxo Bank. “But rather refined product supply, constrained by reduced refinery capacity and output across the Middle East and Russia.”

For decades, the capital’s house prices raced ahead of the national average – but now they are falling in prime areas

A n elegant Georgian facade, a full-width balcony and an exclusive address in South Kensington just steps from the Natural History Museum and the V&A. Yet the listing price of this west London flat at Queen’s Gate Gardens has dropped by nearly £1m since last year, to £4.4m.

It is far from an isolated case. A nearby house originally listed at £20m was slashed to £14m this year, says a local estate agent. In neighbouring Notting Hill, a stucco-fronted property that came to market two years ago at £16m is now being offered for less than £14m, they said.

London’s premium property market is stuck in a rut. While borrowing costs and stretched affordability weigh on everyday buyers , the city’s richest residents are also making deep cuts to the prices of their multimillion-pound homes.

This market is a world away from the rest of the UK property market – where the average house price was just under £275,000 in September , according to Nationwide. The well-heeled neighbourhoods also present a stark contrast with much of the capital, where Londoners struggle to get on to the housing ladder, face rising rents and a lack of affordable housing, and estate agents report the market for flats is now “dead”.

But neighbourhoods such as Knightsbridge, bordering Hyde Park and home to Harrods, are also feeling the pinch, said Harry Dawes, a buying agent based in Belgravia.

“There is a flat on Pont Street, a five-minute walk from Harrods, which sold at £4.4m in 2014, then sold at £3.5m. It can now be bought at £2.5m.”

For decades, London’s property prices raced ahead of the national average. But that gap has been slowly narrowing: while the average price of a UK home rose by about 2% in the year ended in June, prices in inner London boroughs fell by 8.3%, according to the Office for National Statistics.

That drop has been particularly pronounced in Westminster – which includes areas such as Marylebone, Belgravia and Mayfair – with prices down 25.4% year on year. In the City, prices slumped by 20.4%, and in Kensington and Chelsea, prices fell 14.7%.

Properties in the capital became overvalued in the mid-2010s after a period of rapid price growth, said Anthony Payne, the chief executive of the data analyst LonRes. London was then hit hard by Brexit, the Covid pandemic, higher property taxes and a surge in borrowing costs.

Now, owners who bought at the peak now face losses of as much as 25% if they choose to sell, according to estimates from the estate agent Savills.

“London benefited dramatically from international investment and buyers wanting property here as a store of wealth and a way of making money,” Payne said. “These are the people that inflated the market, but now more and more of them are deserting it.”

Jeremy Gee, the managing director at the super-prime estate agent Beauchamp Estates – whose portfolio includes a £42m sub-penthouse overlooking Hyde Park – said the decline had also been driven partly by the exit of super-wealthy groups from the UK, especially after the abolition of the non-dom tax regime.

“There is a section of society who have left the UK recently for lots of reasons, but mainly because of tax,” he said.

“When there are not that many buyers and lots of properties, the prices are going to be softer. Many of our sellers have decided that enough is enough – let’s just sell the property and move on.”

Tax changes have put sellers on edge, too, he added. Last year, the former chancellor Rachel Reeves announced plans for a “mansion tax” on homes worth more than £2m.

This nervousness has triggered a slowdown across the higher tiers of London’s market. Prime properties spent an average of 186 days on the market in the first half of 2026, up from 178 days in the first half of 2025, according to LonRes. Over the same period, the average discount to asking price widened from 8.3% to 10.4% – sellers have grown more likely to accept lowball offers.

Sellers, who normally own these properties for at least a decade, “don’t like it but have to accept it,” said Dawes.

“If they are older, they have to take a lifetime view on their property and accept that from a profit and loss perspective, this last trade might not look good.

“We bought three flats for a client’s kids last year – two in Chelsea and one in Notting Hill – and every seller was selling at a loss.”

Even with multimillion pound discounts propping up on the market, Stuart Bailey, the head of super-prime London sales at the estate agent Knight Frank, said there were still buyers willing to pay above the asking price for “the very best in class” properties.

“A fabulous address, lovely views, immaculate style and newly refurbished,” he said. “It is a matter of premium or discount, retail or trade, brand new or not, and there is nowhere in between. It’s the discounted properties dragging the market down.

“Sellers are more and more realistic about moving on,” he added. “They do not see material price growth on the horizon.”

“With a Labour government the concern is always that there’s going to be some kind of wealth tax somewhere,” he said.

“But many wealthy people also just accept the cost of taxation and that London is simply an expensive city to live in.”

Camilla Dell, a buying agent, said demand is still strong from a wide base of international buyers, including Americans, Singaporeans and Nigerians. Politics, she said, rarely comes up in conversation.

“Most people accept that the UK does not have the best political stability but they want to live here,” she said. “And actually, it helped that Andy Burnham ruled out an overhaul of property taxes in the next budget.”…

Would-be marketers enticed by online talk of entering a world of travel and easy cash find that the reality is rather different

M onths before she entered the Love Island villa, the content creator Yasmin Hadlow promised viewers of her online videos that they could “catch flights and get paid mid-air”. All they had to do, she said, was send her a direct message with the word “freedom”.

The 23-year-old is among several influencers and celebrities, including the former Geordie Shore star Vicky Pattison, working for PlanNet Marketing, which recruits people to work as independent travel agents with a separate US business, InteleTravel.

Pattison’s Instagram page, Vickys Vacays, says it helps women “build confidence, income and freedom through a supportive online travel business”.

It sounds like a great way to make money. But the Guardian has spoken to seven people who were recruited as InteleTravel agents by PlanNet Marketing reps, not the influencers mentioned above, who said they struggled to make money once sign-up costs and monthly fees were taken into account.

Some of them said the people who recruited them encouraged them to sign up as PlanNet Marketing reps and recruit others, and that became their main focus rather than selling holidays.

Mark* always wanted to be a travel agent. He was recruited by a PlanNet rep to work with InteleTravel in 2021 when he was 28. He had just been furloughed during Covid, wanted a career change and was looking at different routes to his dream job.

He paid InteleTravel a sign-up fee of about £150, plus £30 to £40 a month for access to its booking system and training.

Agents earn about 70% of the roughly 10% commission suppliers pay on bookings. So, if they sell £10,000 worth of holidays, the supplier pays out £1,000 in commission and the agent gets £700.

After about 18 months working long days, Mark had only made a handful of sales. “I was making no money on the travel side,” he says, adding that the PlanNet rep who recruited him told him “to try recruitment instead, by signing up with PlanNet Marketing”.

If you are an InteleTravel agent, joining PlanNet Marketing is optional. Those who do so pay PlanNet Marketing a separate monthly fee of about £14. They then get roughly $4, or about £3, for every new person they recruit as an active travel agent, plus referral bonuses and rank-based payouts as their “downline” (number of recruits) grows.

“I ended up with a team of 10 people, but it never felt like me,” Mark says. “The whole point of joining was to be a travel agent, not a recruiter.”

PlanNet Marketing’s annual income disclosure statement suggests earnings from recruitment are typically very low. Its most recent figures show average annual earnings across its general base of representatives are about $40.

Mark was with InteleTravel and PlanNet Marketing for about two years. “I made about three bookings and maybe £1,000 in commission, but I was paying £32 a month in fees, plus about £100 to sign up,” he says. “That wasn’t because I was bad at it. It’s not set up for people to succeed.”

A spokesperson for InteleTravel said: “As with any self-employed business owner, there can be no guarantee of continuous profit and success when starting a business … An unwavering guarantee of significant profit is not a foregone conclusion and cannot be guaranteed, as is the case with any form of self-employment.”

The spokesperson said joining fees covered regulatory licensing and memberships, operational insurance, mandatory training and booking systems, to enable travel advisers to make bookings in accordance with the UK’s travel regulatory requirements.

California’s laws aimed at protecting workers from the impacts of artificial intelligence could pave the way for broader workplace safeguards across the US as calls for regulating the technology mount. They also require companies to notify workers if layoffs were caused by AI and prohibit AI surveillance in workplace bathrooms.

The new laws come as workers increasingly worry whether AI will take their jobs, lead to discrimination and increase workplace surveillance. Unions, worker advocates and even some lawmakers pushed for the new rules, a regulatory shift for a technology that has largely developed unchecked. California , home to many of the leading companies developing AI, represents one of the first states to roll out a sweeping set of workplace regulations targeting the technology.

“It’s a turning point,” said Lorena Gonzalez, president of the California Federation of Labor Unions, AFL-CIO, who’s been helping leaders across the country write regulations. “It’s really the first time we’re seeing California workers showing the country that we don’t have to accept [this].”

Other states that have recently passed individual laws aimed at AI’s use in the workplace include Colorado, Connecticut, Illinois and Texas, narrower in scope than California’s. And more bills across the county are being lined up for consideration, Gonzalez said.

California’s laws aim to target workplace surveillance measures like heat maps that track employees’ movements, including how long they spend in the bathroom, or having their emotional states monitored. Amazon warehouse workers have previously complained about being timed on their bathroom breaks, for example. And at Kaiser Permanente, nurses have said automated systems rated their tone of voice in patient interactions.

But the laws could also prevent future unexpected harms.

“We don’t know all the places companies are using AI, and that is and should be scary,” Gonzalez said.

Part of the strategy for worker advocates and union groups like the California Federation has been following AI companies’ latest products. “If it’s being sold, that’s a good indication” it could be in use, Gonzales said. The federation also plans to use the momentum to revive issues like requiring employers to disclose when they’re using AI in the workplace, which was a bill that died in the state’s assembly appropriations committee this year.

California’s new laws are a key step in gaining regulatory ground for worker advocates, said Robin Feldman, director and founder of AI Law & Innovation Institute at The University of California College of the Law, San Francisco. Still, the statutes are somewhat limited in how they are implemented.

“The bills have no private enforcement,” Feldman said. “In other words: workers can’t sue. Only the government can enforce the laws.”

The new regulations come amid a backdrop of record AI spending at big tech companies along with massive job cuts. But workers have started pushing back. Indian government issued with warning it would be in contempt of court if it failed to release Jagtar Singh Johal

The British Sikh activist Jagtar Singh Johal has been released from a Delhi prison after the Indian high court warned the government it would be found in contempt of court if it continued to attempt to keep him in jail despite an 18 September court order releasing him on bail. Johal has been incarcerated for nine years without any full trial.

The court order was issued after Johal’s lawyers issued a writ of habeas corpus alleging he was being detained against the express direction of the court.

Johal’s nine-year detention on alleged terrorist offences, has been a cause of diplomatic tension between the UK and India, but campaigners have claimed the British government has not been active enough to secure his release or, alternatively, a full trial.

The campaign group Reprieve says his case has never come to full trial largely because of the inability of the Indian government to assemble credible witnesses to back their claim that Johal transported £3,000 to France to fund a multinational extremist plot involving targeted killings in the Punjab in 2016-17.

On Thursday morning, the high court in Delhi instructed the Indian government to release Johal by 2.30pm Indian time, giving government officials three hours to comply or find themselves risking contempt proceedings. In the end, he was released in the late afternoon wearing a red T-shirt to be greeted by friends, family and flowers.

Documents shown to the court by Johal’s lawyers on behalf of his father-in-law as petitioner revealed that messages from the prison to the Ministry of Home Affairs seeking permission for his release had been left unanswered.

His lawyers in their petition stated he had met all the bail conditions yet “the detainee has nevertheless not been released, and is being held in custody without the authority of any court, pending a ‘clarification’ sought by the jail from the Ministry of Home Affairs”.

The petition added that no clarification from the ministry had been forthcoming, explaining: “Every day of such detention is a continuing violation of the detainee’s fundamental rights under article 21 of the constitution of India.”

Johal has been detained by Indian authorities since 4 November 2017. He is facing eight charges of terrorism in the federal court, but had been cleared of largely similar charges by a Punjab court. He claims any initial confessions he gave were extracted under torture.

The bail terms last week imposed 11 conditions, including surrender of passport, a personal bond of 500,000 Indian rupees (£3,930) with two sureties, fortnightly reporting to the investigating officer, prior intimation of any change of residence and a ban on travelling to the Punjab. He was also restricted from talking to media about the case directly or indirectly.

The Indian government has alleged the Khalistan Liberation Force undertook the killings and Johal had “complete knowledge of the conspiracy” and was a KLF member.

His Dumbarton-based brother Gurpreet Singh Johal said: “There have been so many setbacks and disappointments in the last nine years that I didn’t dare to believe it until I saw Jagtar walking out of the prison gates with my own eyes. The last two weeks have been torture – knowing that Jagtar had been granted bail, but the authorities were refusing to let him out. I’ll sleep well tonight, knowing that he’s not behind bars.

“Tomorrow morning, the fight continues, because he’s still on trial and facing the death penalty for something he didn’t do, trapped in a sham legal process designed to punish him for standing up for human rights”.

Reprieve’s deputy executive director, Dan Dolan, said: “While tonight is the first night in almost nine years that Jagtar Singh Johal is not caged in a prison cell, he still has the threat of a death sentence hanging over him. It should also be noted that, despite bail being ordered, the prison refused to release Jagtar until his family brought a habeas corpus petition and a judge warned the jail they’d be found in contempt of court”.

Experts sceptical flydubai co-pilot’s only motivation was to end his own life and say key question is means of radicalisation

Many of the details of what happened on flight FZ 1073 are still unclear, but what happened next is well documented by witness testimony and videos.

As the plane went into a steep dive, losing 16,000ft of altitude in about a minute, most of the 182 passengers screamed, prayed and tried desperately to reassure panicking children. But a small group rushed to the cockpit and overpowered the co-pilot. One, a plumber, copied an action seen on TV documentaries about plane crashes to pull the aircraft out of its dive.

Two off-duty pilots on the flight, both among the handful of non-Israeli passengers, then took over the controls of the now almost rudderless aircraft to guide it eventually to a landing 90 minutes later in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. In Israel, there is little doubt about the co-pilot’s intentions. “The co-pilot is a terrorist who tried either to hijack the plane or bring it down as a suicide. Suggestions that the crash of an AirIndia 787 in Ahmedabad last year was the result of a pilot deliberately cutting fuel to engines have been fiercely disputed .

Terrorism experts are sceptical that the flydubai co-pilot’s only motivation was to end his own life. “The odds that a pilot would decide to commit suicide and just happen to be flying a plane full of Israelis are pretty low,” said Colin Clarke, a terrorism expert at the respected Soufan Center in New York.

“Netanyahu has a big interest in this being terrorism, but the best explanation is probably the most obvious one [ie terrorism],” he said. “The question … is: was [the co-pilot] recruited by a group or an organisation … or was he radicalised alone? In which case, what was hyping him up, given he was flying a planeload of Israelis? Could that be Gaza?”

Security services have been warning of a wave of radicalisation across the Middle East prompted by the war in Gaza, which came to an inconclusive halt with a fragile ceasefire a year ago. But there has been limited evidence as yet that any violent Islamist extremist groups have gained support as a consequence of the conflict.

Terrorism experts said the most obvious group that might be involved in such an attack would be al-Qaida in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP), which is based in Yemen and has a history of efforts to bring down planes. They said AQAP had recently sought to launch or inspire violence internationally.

“Aviation remains the classic propaganda by deed,” Clarke said. “It’s been said that terrorism is theatre, and nothing is more theatrical than taking down an airplane. Speculation that Flávio Bolsonaro will try to strip Our Lady of Aparecida of position could become deciding factor in run-up to Sunday

He recalled a major outcry in 1995 when a neo-Pentecostal pastor kicked a statue of Our Lady of Aparecida on TV.

Simas believed religious racism was at the heart of the outcry, given that Our Lady of Aparecida was a black representation of the Virgin Mary. “When all of this comes into contact with a turbulent political context, in a country experiencing the tensions of a highly contested pre-election scenario, all these controversies come to the surface,” Simas added.

With 40 dead and a disaster declared across all 50 city districts, experts warn extreme flooding will only worsen across south-east Asia

B angkok is used to absorbing the sudden afternoon downpours that inundate the city during the rainy season. Even streets in many central high-rise districts can briefly turn into rivers, with rats and cockroaches racing out of sewers and taking temporary refuge on trees and buildings as the subterranean world is flushed out.

But every city has a breaking point, and this year rain fell so fast and so hard that whole neighbourhoods of the Thai capital have been transformed, not into rivers, but stagnant lakes. In parts of the city, roughly 300mm of rain – the equivalent of half a year of average rainfall in London – fell in about two days.

About 40 people died in flood-related incidents, according to the government. A number of the deaths were from drowning and several from accidental electrocution. Thousands of people stayed in more than 230 shelters across the city, authorities said.

Suleemas Kurangkul, a 73-year-old resident of a block of flats whose ground floor stairs are still under water, said last weekend’s rain was not the usual evening storm but was constant, “like all day, all night”.

“The water just kept rising,” said Suleemas, whose flat is above the waterline on the second floor. By the time she and her neighbours received a mobile phone warning, it was too late, and the street-level water was waist-high.

The 1970s Khlong Chan flat compound in north-east Bangkok where Suleemas lives has become a symbol of the disaster. Photos have been shared across Thailand of the flats rising out of the brownish water, with the rooftops of parked cars barely peeking above the surface, although the authorities had managed to drain away the worst of it by Thursday.

Later in the week, during a brief respite in the rain, Suleemas said the water had receded somewhat. “People are so happy to see the sunshine,” she said. “Yet, the smell is getting stronger. So much debris and rubbish floating all over the place.”

Built on a vast floodplain of the Chao Phraya River, Bangkok, a megacity of millions, relies on a network of muddy canals to drain water, as well as pumps and dikes. But concrete construction has destroyed much of the canal network, and the city is unable to cope.

The government has declared a flood disaster across all 50 of the city’s districts. Some neighbourhoods have turned into dystopian scenes, with people using blow-up paddling pools or, in one case, a floating fridge, as boats to reach their homes. One man was arrested for riding a jetski along a main road.

“It’s a lesson,” said Chaleerat Chamrasporn, 55, a resident. “The kids are into doomsday-themed content, so now they can see what the ‘end of the world’ is actually like, or rather, that this is just the beginning.”

Flooding has also disrupted Bangkok’s main Suvarnabhumi airport, with about half ⁠of Thai Airways’ workforce unable to report for work at one point this week, causing thousands of items of luggage ​to pile up and forcing flight ​cancellations. Many schools have closed, and with much of the capital in gridlock even people in less affected areas have been stuck at home.

Thailand’s prime minister, Anutin Charnvirakul, told reporters that Bangkok’s metropolitan area was still at risk from flood waters flowing in from ​the north, and said a war room had ‌been set up to monitor ‌the situation. Thailand’s weather ⁠agency has forecast more ​heavy rain for next week.

It is part of a pattern that seems to be setting in this part of the world. South-east Asia has already seen a worsening of extreme floods, scientists say, a trend that is set to worsen as fossil fuel pollutants bake the planet further. Hot seas evaporate more water and warm air can hold more moisture, allowing downpours to crash down with far more force.

“In central Thailand, I can see from my maps, we have already seen a small but significant trend towards extreme rainfall,” said Nikolaos Skliris, an ocean scientist at the University of Southampton who has studied heavy rain in the region. “In the long-term, all models show this will be amplified – more rainfall, and more extreme rainfall.”

It is too early for scientists to attribute these particular rains to climate breakdown without doing a study. They were caused by a low-pressure system that moved from an unusually warm South China Sea over Cambodia and Vietnam before getting stuck above Bangkok, which was fairly cool, data from Copernicus Climate Pulse showed.

The picture is complicated by the emergence of an abnormally strong El Niño, a cyclical weather pattern that brings record heat and more violent extremes around the world. Its presence typically leads to drier summer conditions in south-east Asia but recent research suggests it still exacerbates days with extreme rainfall.

Naim Laeni, a consultant and part-time university lecturer who co-authored a study on Bangkok’s flood resilience , said authorities had underestimated the strength of the rains, which persisted for days. The city’s drainage canals can handle about 60mm of rain an hour, rising to 80mm in upgraded sections, but localised bursts exceeded this while leaving too little time between periods of stress.

“The government did not communicate the seriousness,” said Laeni. “Usually in Bangkok we receive heavy rain for a few hours, not for days.”

Neighbouring Myanmar has suffered from the same weather system, with flash floods and blocked roads complicating rescue efforts in the country.

‘No one disrespects Our Lady’: fears for Brazil’s patron saint grip country ahead of election

S hortly after his controversial speech to the United Nations general assembly in September, Donald Trump gathered a dozen like-minded Latin American leaders and boasted that rightwing candidates had won all seven presidential elections held in the region since he began his second term.

“Everybody I’ve endorsed has won,” the US president said in New York to most of the leaders of the Shield of the Americas, an anti-drug cartel coalition of 15 countries governed by the right or far right.

Those electoral victories – and the US takeover of Venezuela after capturing Nicolás Maduro – have left just six Latin American countries under leftwing governments: regional heavyweights Brazil and Mexico, small Uruguay and Guatemala, and the isolated regimes of Cuba and Nicaragua.

On Sunday, Brazilians go to the polls in a presidential election that many believe will determine more than Latin America’s largest country’s fate for the next four years.

Given Mexico’s geographic proximity and unique economic relationship with the US, analysts see Brazil as perhaps the last country in the region still capable of saying “no” to Trump’s whims – something that could change dramatically depending on the election result.

Polls indicate a neck-and-neck race between Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the 80-year-old leftist incumbent who is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term, and Flávio Bolsonaro , 45, the far-right senator son of former president Jair Bolsonaro.

“Trump really does take seriously the idea that the Americas should be his back yard,” said Pedro Telles, a professor at the School of International Relations at Brazil’s FGV university.

“Mexico will remain relevant, and its president, Claudia Sheinbaum , is one of the most popular leftwing leaders. But if Flávio wins, it would be a real blow to the left and a major boost to the far-right agenda globally,” added Telles.

“There is a lot at stake,” said Sandra Borda Guzmán, an associate professor of political science at Colombia’s Universidad de los Andes. “Instead of taking the opportunity to expand our region’s autonomy, a far-right victory would align the region unconditionally with the dictates of the US,” she added.

Lula and Bolsonaro differ sharply on the US, including over what has become Trump’s main foreign policy for the region: the so-called “war on drugs ” used to justify dozens of airstrikes on boats that have killed more than 230 people and joint operations involving US military personnel on land .

While Bolsonaro has pledged to join the Shield of the Americas and to follow an “iron fist” approach to crime, Lula has raised concerns about sovereignty and said it is “sad to see the inferiority complex of Latin American presidents” who are part of the Trump-created coalition.

Lula and Trump’s relationship has swung between not speaking and public displays of warmth , but it is currently at a low point , with the Brazilian president and Democratic members of the US Congress accusing Washington of trying to interfere in Bolsonaro’s favour.

“Brazil is a big prize,” said Michael Shifter, adjunct professor at Georgetown University’s School of Foreign Service, adding that amid endless conflicts in Iran, Ukraine and Israel-Palestine, “US foreign policy is going very badly in the rest of the world.”

A victory for Bolsonaro in Brazil, he said, would be used “triumphantly” by Trump for producing an “almost completely aligned region”.

At the latest Shield of the Americas meeting, Trump made clear that it was not all about security. The US president also referred to the “tremendous natural wealth” of Latin American countries, which he said could not “be taken over by hostile outside powers” – widely understood as a reference to China.

Privileged access to Brazil’s rare earths and critical minerals was one of the conditions Washington imposed in exchange for not applying tariffs, which Lula rejected. Bolsonaro, on the other hand, has offered those natural resources as the “solution” to help the US “break its dependence on China”.

“Democracy is also kind of on the line here,” added Shifter, noting that Bolsonaro was only running because his father cannot – Jair Bolsonaro is under house arrest after being convicted of attempting a coup to overturn his defeat by Lula in the 2022 election.

“So it’s not just a question of one more country moving to the right, but of a right that has a very problematic relationship with democracy,” he said.

As in recent elections across Latin America, the race includes other candidates but is polarised between two leading candidates. Lula and Bolsonaro have alternated as frontrunners in the final stretch, making the outcome unpredictable; if neither wins 50% plus one of the votes, there will be a runoff on 25 October.

Bolsonaro’s only previous bid for an executive role in government ended ignominiously when he took fourth place in Rio’s 2016 mayoral race. But analysts say there are several reasons why a congressman best known for his family name and corruption allegations – some shelved , others still under investigation – has emerged as a serious challenger to a three-time president.

Unemployment, poverty and inflation have fallen , and average incomes have risen, but so has household debt – something many attribute to online betting, which the older Bolsonaro left unregulated and Lula banned days before the vote.

The incumbent’s campaign has also been hit by corruption allegations – still under investigation – involving his son and a former aide, while a scandal involving supreme court justices with no connection to Lula may have rubbed off on the president.
